P5. Sum the possible values of k.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] From the given equal ratios, write a=k(1-b), b=k(1-c), c=k(1-a), equivalently
a+kb=k, b+kc=k, c+ka=k.
S2. [derive] Subtracting consecutive equations gives
a-b+k(b-c)=0, b-c+k(c-a)=0, c-a+k(a-b)=0.
S3. [derive] Let x=a-b, y=b-c, z=c-a. Then x=-ky, y=-kz, z=-kx. Since a,b,c are distinct, at least one of x,y,z is nonzero. Combining the relations gives x=-k^3 x, so 1+k^3=0. Thus k^3=-1.
S4. [derive] The cube roots of -1 are -1, (1+i\sqrt{3})/2, and (1-i\sqrt{3})/2. If k=-1, the equations become a-b=-1, b-c=-1, c-a=-1. Adding them gives 0=-3, a contradiction. Hence k is one of the two roots of k^2-k+1=0.

Direct substitution gives a+kb=k, b+kc=1+k^2=k, and c+ka=1+k+k^3=k. Thus both roots of k^2-k+1=0 are possible values of k.
S6. [calc] The sum of the roots of k^2-k+1=0 is -(-1)/1 -> <<-(-1)/1=1>>.

[Check]

V2. The excluded value k=-1 gives contradictory equations, while the explicit construction in S5 satisfies all three equations and the denominator conditions.

S2. [derive] Compute the squared modulus |a omega + b|^2 = (a omega + b)(a conjugate(omega) + b) = a^2 + b^2 + ab(omega + conjugate(omega)).

[Answer]

[Plan]

P2. Set the squared distance to the focus equal to the squared distance to the directrix.
P3. Clear the denominator from the distance-to-line formula.
P4. Expand and collect like terms.
P5. Normalize and verify the integer coefficients.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let (x,y) be any point on the parabola. Its distance to the focus (3,3) equals its distance to the line 3x+7y=21.
S2. [derive] The squared distance to the focus is (x-3)^2+(y-3)^2, and the squared distance to the directrix is (3x+7y-21)^2/(3^2+7^2).
S3. [derive] Since 3^2+7^2=58, equate the squared distances: (x-3)^2+(y-3)^2 = (3x+7y-21)^2/58.
S4. [derive] Multiply both sides by 58 to obtain 58[(x-3)^2+(y-3)^2] = (3x+7y-21)^2.
S5. [symbolic] Expand the left side -> {{58[(x-3)^2+(y-3)^2] => 58x^2 + 58y^2 - 348x - 348y + 1044}}
S6. [symbolic] Expand the right side -> {{(3x+7y-21)^2 => 9x^2 + 42xy + 49y^2 - 126x - 294y + 441}}
S7. [derive] Move the right side to the left side: 58x^2+58y^2-348x-348y+1044-(9x^2+42xy+49y^2-126x-294y+441)=0.
S8. [symbolic] Combine like terms -> {{58x^2+58y^2-348x-348y+1044-(9x^2+42xy+49y^2-126x-294y+441) => 49x^2 - 42xy + 9y^2 - 222x - 54y + 603}}
S9. [derive] Thus the parabola has equation 49x^2 - 42xy + 9y^2 - 222x - 54y + 603 = 0.

[Check]
V1. The equation was obtained by equating squared distances and clearing the positive denominator 58, so the equivalence is preserved.
V2. The coefficient of x^2 is 49, which is positive.
V3. The coefficient gcd is gcd(49,42,9,222,54,603)=1, so the equation is normalized.

[Answer]
\boxed{49x^2 - 42xy + 9y^2 - 222x - 54y + 603 = 0}

This is a quadratic-vertex and intersection problem. The goal is to find a+c. The key idea is to write both parabolas in vertex form with the same minimum value, use the root conditions to relate the vertices, and use the common intersection point.

[Plan]
P1. Express f and g in vertex form using the x-coordinates of their vertices.
P2. Use the condition that each vertex x-coordinate is a root of the other polynomial.
P3. Use the common minimum value to relate the vertex heights.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let the vertex x-coordinate of f be p=-a/2 and the vertex x-coordinate of g be q=-c/2. Since both have the same minimum value m, write f(x)=(x-p)^2+m and g(x)=(x-q)^2+m, with p != q.
S2. [derive] The condition that p is a root of g and q is a root of f gives g(p)=(p-q)^2+m=0 and f(q)=(q-p)^2+m=0, so m=-(p-q)^2.
S3. [derive] Since the graphs intersect at (100,-100), both equations hold: (100-p)^2+m=-100 and (100-q)^2+m=-100.
S4. [derive] Subtract the two equations from S3 to get (100-p)^2=(100-q)^2.
S5. [case] Since p != q, equality of squares requires 100-p=-(100-q), so p+q=200.
S6. [symbolic] Since a=-2p and c=-2q, use p+q=200 -> {{a+c = -2(p+q) => a+c = -400}}

S3. [symbolic] Complete the cube -> {{t^3-3t^2+3t-3 => (t-1)^3-2}}
S4. [derive] Since f(a)=0, the real number a satisfies (a-1)^3-2=0, hence (a-1)^3=2.
S5. [theorem] The equation z^3=2 has exactly one real solution, z=\sqrt[3]{2}, and two nonreal complex solutions.
S6. [derive] Because a is real, it must equal the real solution of (a-1)^3=2.

S1. [setup] Let f(x) = sum_{i=0}^n a_i x^i with a_i >= 0, and define b_i = a_i 6^i. Then b_i >= 0 and sum_i b_i = f(6) = 24.
S2. [derive] The condition f(24) = 1536 becomes sum_i b_i 4^i = 1536. Therefore the weighted average of the values 4^i with weights b_i is (sum_i b_i 4^i) / (sum_i b_i) = 1536/24 = 64.
S3. [derive] Also, f(12) = sum_i a_i 12^i = sum_i b_i (12/6)^i = sum_i b_i 2^i = sum_i b_i sqrt(4^i).
S4. [theorem] Since sqrt(t) is concave, Jensen's inequality gives (sum_i b_i sqrt(4^i)) / (sum_i b_i) <= sqrt((sum_i b_i 4^i) / (sum_i b_i)).
S5. [calc] Substitute the total mass 24 and the weighted average 64 -> <<24*sqrt(64)=192>>, so f(12) <= 192.
S6. [setup] Equality in Jensen's inequality for the strictly concave function sqrt(t) occurs only when all positive-weight terms have the same value of 4^i. Since the weighted average is 64, this requires 4^i = 64, so i = 3.
S7. [calc] Thus b_3 = 24 and a_3 = b_3 / 6^3 -> <<24/216=1/9>>.
S8. [derive] Hence the extremal polynomial is f(x) = (1/9)x^3. It has nonnegative coefficients and attains f(12) = (1/9) * 12^3 = 192.

V2. Substitute x = 24 into f(x) = x^3/9 -> <<24^3/9=1536>>.

[Answer]

[Overview]
This is an algebraic roots/reversal problem. The goal is to count possible multisets of ten integer roots. The key idea is that reversing coefficients sends each nonzero root r to 1/r, so the root multiset must be unchanged under r -> 1/r.

[Plan]
P1. Use the reversed polynomial relation to identify the roots of the reversed polynomial.
P2. Translate the condition into an invariance condition on the root multiset.
P3. Use integrality to determine which integer roots can occur.
P4. Count all multisets of ten roots using the allowed values.
P5. Verify that every counted multiset can actually occur.
P6. Confirm the nonzero leading and constant coefficient conditions.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let P(x)=a_{10}x^{10}+a_9x^9+...+a_0 and let its root multiset be S={r_1,...,r_10}. Since a_0 is nonzero, none of the roots is 0.
S2. [derive] The reversed polynomial is Q(x)=a_0x^{10}+a_1x^9+...+a_{10}. Also Q(x)=x^{10}P(1/x), so for x nonzero, Q(x)=0 if and only if P(1/x)=0. Hence the roots of Q are exactly 1/r_1,1/r_2,...,1/r_10, counted with multiplicity.
S3. [derive] Since Q has the same root multiset S, the multiset S must satisfy S={1/r : r in S}. Thus every root r in S has its reciprocal 1/r also in S with the same total multiplicities.
S4. [theorem] Each root r is an integer. For 1/r to be an integer, we must have r dividing 1, so r=1 or r=-1.
S5. [calc] A multiset of ten roots using only 1 and -1 is determined by the number of occurrences of -1, which can range from 0 to 10. Therefore the number of such multisets is <<10+1=11>>.
S6. [derive] Each of these multisets is attainable. If there are k roots equal to 1 and 10-k roots equal to -1, take P(x)=(x-1)^k(x+1)^{10-k}. This has integer coefficients, nonzero leading and constant coefficients, and its roots are closed under reciprocal because 1 and -1 are self-reciprocal.

[Check]
V1. For every k=0,1,...,10, the polynomial (x-1)^k(x+1)^{10-k} has roots only 1 and -1, and their reciprocals are again 1 and -1, so the reversed polynomial has the same root multiset.
V2. No other integer root can occur, since an integer r whose reciprocal must also be an integer must satisfy r=1 or r=-1. Thus the count 11 is complete.

[Answer]
\boxed{11}

[Overview]
This is an assignment optimization problem on an 8 by 8 board. The goal is to choose one square in each row and each column so that the sum of the reciprocal labels is minimized. The key idea is that the denominators of the selected labels have a fixed total sum, so the reciprocal sum is minimized when those denominators are as equal as possible.

[Plan]
P1. Set up coordinates for rows and columns and rewrite each label in terms of these coordinates.
P2. Express the sum of the denominators of any valid selection.
P3. Use an inequality for reciprocals with fixed denominator sum.
P4. Determine when equality is possible and construct a valid selection.
P5. Compute the minimum sum.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Number columns from left to right by i = 0,1,...,7 and rows from top to bottom by t = 0,1,...,7. The square in column i and row t has label 1/(i+t+1).
S2. [derive] A valid selection has one square in each row and column, so if the chosen square in row t is column i_t, then i_0,i_1,...,i_7 is a permutation of 0,1,...,7. The sum D of the denominators is D = sum_{t=0}^7 (i_t+t+1) = (0+1+...+7) + (1+2+...+8) = 28+36 = 64.
S3. [theorem] For positive numbers d_1,...,d_8, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives (sum d_t)(sum 1/d_t) >= 8^2 = 64.
S4. [derive] Since D = sum d_t = 64, the sum of labels satisfies sum 1/d_t >= 64/64 = 1.
S5. [case] Equality occurs when all denominators d_t are equal. Since their sum is 64, each must equal 8. This is achieved by choosing the anti-diagonal squares with i_t = 7-t, because then i_t+t+1 = (7-t)+t+1 = 8.
S6. [calc] The sum of labels for this valid selection is -> <<8*(1/8)=1>>

[Check]
V1. The anti-diagonal selection uses each column exactly once because i_t = 7-t runs through 0,1,...,7.
V2. The denominator sum for that selection is 8+8+...+8 = 64, and the reciprocal sum is 8*(1/8)=1.
V3. The inequality shows no valid selection can have reciprocal sum below 1.

[Answer]
\boxed{1}

P5. Verify the resulting ordered pair.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let the intersection point be (a,b). Since it lies on y=f(x), we have b=f(a). Since it lies on y=f^{-1}(x), we have a=f(b).
S2. [derive] Compute f'(x)=3x^2+12x+16=3(x+2)^2+4>0 for all real x, so f is strictly increasing.
S3. [theorem] For a strictly increasing function, an intersection of y=f(x) and y=f^{-1}(x) must lie on y=x. Indeed, if a<b, then b=f(a)<f(b)=a, a contradiction; similarly a>b is impossible.
S4. [derive] Therefore a=b, and the point satisfies f(a)=a. So solve f(x)=x.
S5. [symbolic] Set f(x)=x and simplify -> {{x^3 + 6x^2 + 16x + 28 = x => x^3 + 6x^2 + 15x + 28 = 0}}
S6. [symbolic] Factor the cubic -> {{x^3 + 6x^2 + 15x + 28 => (x + 4)(x^2 + 2x + 7)}}

V3. Strict monotonicity guarantees there cannot be another intersection point, matching the uniqueness stated in the problem.

[Answer]

S8. [calc] Check x = 6 -> <<6^4-625=671>>
S9. [calc] Check x = 7 -> <<7^4-625=1776>>

This is a floor-equation problem. The goal is to find all real x satisfying the nested floor equation. The key idea is to simplify the nested floor and write x using its integer part and fractional part.

[Plan]
P1. Simplify the nested floor expression and the right-hand side.
P2. Rewrite the equation as a relation involving floor(2x) and floor(x).
P3. Let x be the sum of its integer part and fractional part.
P4. Split into cases according to the value of floor(2t).
P5. Combine the resulting intervals and check endpoints.

[Solution]
S1. [theorem] For every integer N, floor(N - 1/2) = N - 1, and for every real x, floor(x + 2) = floor(x) + 2.
S2. [derive] Taking N = floor(2x), the original equation becomes floor(2x) - 1 = floor(x) + 2, so floor(2x) - floor(x) = 3.
S3. [setup] Write x = m + t, where m = floor(x) is an integer and 0 <= t < 1 is the fractional part.
S4. [derive] Then floor(2x) = 2m + floor(2t), so floor(2x) - floor(x) = m + floor(2t). Thus m + floor(2t) = 3.
S5. [case] Since 0 <= t < 1, we have floor(2t) = 0 when 0 <= t < 1/2, and floor(2t) = 1 when 1/2 <= t < 1.
S6. [case] If floor(2t) = 0, then m = 3 and 0 <= t < 1/2, giving 3 <= x < 7/2.
S7. [case] If floor(2t) = 1, then m = 2 and 1/2 <= t < 1, giving 5/2 <= x < 3.
S8. [derive] Taking the union of the two cases gives 5/2 <= x < 7/2.

[Check]
V1. At x = 5/2, floor(2x) = 5, so the left side is floor(5 - 1/2) = 4, while floor(x + 2) = floor(9/2) = 4.
V2. At x = 7/2, floor(2x) = 7, so the left side is floor(7 - 1/2) = 6, while floor(x + 2) = floor(11/2) = 5, so x = 7/2 must be excluded.
V3. At x = 3, floor(2x) = 6, so the left side is floor(6 - 1/2) = 5, while floor(x + 2) = floor(5) = 5, so x = 3 is included.

[Answer]
\boxed{\left[\frac{5}{2},\frac{7}{2}\right)}

S6. [derive] Expanding and rearranging gives 3x^2 + 3y^2 - 2x - 1 = 0.
S7. [derive] Dividing by 3 and completing the square gives (x - 1/3)^2 + y^2 = 4/9.

V3. The modulus condition |z + 1| = 2|z| is equivalent to the circle equation found, so all roots lie on this circle.

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{2}{3}}

This is a complex roots-of-unity problem. The goal is to compute a finite sum of even powers of a nontrivial seventh root of unity. The key idea is to recognize the exponents as an arithmetic progression and use the geometric-series formula together with omega^7 = 1.

[Plan]
P1. Write the sum as a finite geometric series.
P2. Reduce exponents modulo 7 using omega^7 = 1.
P3. Simplify the geometric-series expression.
P4. Verify the result by a residue-counting or algebraic sanity check.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let S = omega^16 + omega^18 + omega^20 + ... + omega^54 = sum_{k=0}^{19} omega^(16+2k). Since omega^7 = 1 and omega != 1, omega has order 7, so 1 - omega^2 != 0.
S2. [symbolic] Apply the finite geometric-series formula -> {{S = omega^16 (1 - (omega^2)^20)/(1 - omega^2) => S = omega^16 (1 - omega^40)/(1 - omega^2)}}
S3. [derive] Reduce exponents using omega^7 = 1: omega^40 = omega^(35+5) = omega^5 and omega^16 = omega^(14+2) = omega^2.
S4. [symbolic] Substitute these reductions into the geometric sum -> {{S = omega^2 (1 - omega^5)/(1 - omega^2) => S = (omega^2 - omega^7)/(1 - omega^2)}}
S5. [symbolic] Use omega^7 = 1 and simplify -> {{S = (omega^2 - 1)/(1 - omega^2) => S = -1}}

[Check]
V1. The 20 exponents modulo 7 consist of two full cycles of the seven seventh roots plus the six nonzero residues 2,4,6,1,3,5. The two full cycles sum to 0, and the remaining six nonzero seventh roots sum to -1.
V2. The geometric-series simplification gives (omega^2 - 1)/(1 - omega^2) = -1, which agrees with the residue-counting check.

[Answer]
\boxed{-1}

solution:
[Overview]
This is a piecewise-linear locus problem. The goal is the total length of all line segments forming the set S. The key idea is to write the equation as h(x)+h(y)=1, analyze the piecewise-linear function h, and count the resulting line segments by their horizontal projections.

[Plan]
P1. Define a function h(t) so that S is given by h(x)+h(y)=1.
P2. Find the piecewise formula and critical points of h(t).
P3. Determine how many y-values satisfy h(y)=1-h(x) for a generic x.
P4. Sum the lengths of the resulting slope +1 or -1 line segments over each x-interval.
P5. Combine the contributions to get the total length.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let h(t)=||\,|t|-2\,|-1|. Then S is the set of points satisfying h(x)+h(y)=1.
S2. [derive] For t>=0, h(t)=|\,|t-2|-1|, so
h(t)=1-t on [0,1],
h(t)=t-1 on [1,2],
h(t)=3-t on [2,3],
h(t)=t-3 on [3,infinity].
The function h is even, and h(t)<=1 exactly when |t|<=4.
S3. [derive] For any r with 0<r<1, the equation h(t)=r has exactly eight solutions:
t=-(1-r), -(1+r), -(3-r), -(3+r), 1-r, 1+r, 3-r, 3+r.
S4. [derive] The interval [-4,4] is split by the critical points -4,-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3,4 into 8 unit intervals. On each such interval, h maps the x-interval onto (0,1), so for each generic x there are exactly 8 corresponding y-values from S3. Each branch is a line segment of slope +1 or -1, hence its length equals sqrt(2) times its horizontal projection.
S5. [calc] Each unit x-interval contributes 8*sqrt(2), and there are 8 such intervals, so the total length is <<sqrt(2)*8*8=64\sqrt{2}>>.

[Check]
V1. On one unit interval such as (-4,-3), h(x) runs from 1 to 0, giving 8 y-branches of slope +1 or -1 across horizontal width 1, so that interval contributes 8*sqrt(2).
V2. There are 8 unit intervals in [-4,4], so the total length is 8*(8*sqrt(2))=64*sqrt(2), matching the calculation.

[Answer]
\boxed{64\sqrt{2}}

solution:
[Overview]
This is an optimization problem for a right triangular prism. The goal is to maximize the volume given that the sum of two adjacent lateral face areas and one base area is 24. The key idea is to express the volume in terms of the base area and the sum of two adjacent base edges, then use an area bound and single-variable maximization.

[Plan]
P1. Define the two base edges meeting at the chosen vertex, the included angle, and the prism height.
P2. Express the given area sum and the prism volume.
P3. Use the bound on the area of a triangle with two sides having a fixed sum.
P4. Maximize the resulting one-variable volume bound.
P5. Verify that equality is attainable and compute the maximum volume.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let a and b be the two base edges meeting at the chosen base vertex, let theta be their included angle, and let h be the prism height. Put S=a+b and K=(1/2)ab sin(theta), the base area.
S2. [setup] The two adjacent lateral face areas are h a and h b, while the adjacent base area is K. Thus hS + K = 24, and the volume is V=K h.
S3. [derive] For fixed S=a+b, the base area satisfies K=(1/2)ab sin(theta) <= S^2/8, with equality when a=b=S/2 and theta=90 degrees. Hence S >= sqrt(8K).
S4. [derive] From hS+K=24, we have h=(24-K)/S. Therefore V=K(24-K)/S <= K(24-K)/sqrt(8K)=(24-K)sqrt(K/8).
S5. [symbolic] Differentiate the bounding function f(K)=(24-K)sqrt(K/8) and locate its critical point -> {{f'(K)=0 => K=8}}.
S6. [derive] Since f(K) increases on 0<K<8 and decreases on 8<K<24, its maximum occurs at K=8.
S7. [calc] Compute the maximum bound -> <<(24-8)*sqrt(8/8)=16>>.
S8. [derive] Equality is attainable with K=8, S=8, a=b=4, theta=90 degrees, and h=(24-8)/8=2.
S9. [calc] The volume at equality is -> <<8*2=16>>.

[Check]
V1. The two lateral face areas are both 2*4=8, and the base area is (1/2)*4*4=8, so the required sum is <<8+8+8=24>>.
V2. The optimal prism has base area 8 and height 2, so its volume is <<8*2=16>>.

[Answer]
\boxed{16}

solution:
[Overview]
This is a rational-function asymptotics problem. The goal is to find the largest possible degree of the numerator polynomial q(x) so that the graph still has a horizontal asymptote. The key idea is to compare the degree of the numerator with the fixed denominator degree, including the possibility of canceling common factors.

[Plan]
P1. Let D(x) be the fixed denominator polynomial and note that its degree is 5.
P2. Relate the existence of a horizontal asymptote to the degrees of the numerator and denominator after canceling common factors.
P3. Derive an upper bound on the degree of q(x).
P4. Show that the upper bound is attainable.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let D(x)=2x^5+x^4-7x^2+1 and let deg q = m. Let g(x)=gcd(q(x),D(x)) have degree k.
S2. [theorem] A rational function has a horizontal asymptote only if, after common factors are canceled, the numerator degree is at most the denominator degree.
S3. [derive] After cancellation, the numerator degree is m-k and the denominator degree is 5-k. Thus the condition is m-k <= 5-k, so m <= 5.
S4. [calc] The bound is attainable by choosing q(x)=2x^5, whose degree is <<5=5>>.
S5. [symbolic] For this choice, the rational function becomes -> {{(2x^5)/(2x^5+x^4-7x^2+1) => 1/(1+1/x-7/x^3+1/x^5)}}
S6. [calc] As x tends to positive or negative infinity, the expression approaches <<1/(1+0-0+0)=1>>, so the graph has horizontal asymptote y=1.

[Check]
V1. The cancellation argument gives m <= 5 for any common factor degree k.
V2. The example q(x)=2x^5 has degree 5 and produces a horizontal asymptote, so no larger finite degree is possible.

[Answer]
\boxed{5}

[Overview]
This is an algebraic inequality problem involving logarithms. The goal is to find x^{sqrt{2}} + y^{sqrt{2}} from the given equation. The key idea is to set a = log_2 x and b = log_3 y, then apply AM-GM to force equality at a = b = sqrt{2}.

[Plan]
P1. Define a = log_2 x and b = log_3 y, and note a,b > 0.
P2. Rewrite the given equation as a^4 + b^4 + 8 = 8ab.
P3. Apply AM-GM to a^4, b^4, 4, 4 to show a^4 + b^4 + 8 >= 8ab.
P4. Use the equality condition to find a and b.
P5. Compute x^{sqrt{2}} + y^{sqrt{2}}.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let a = log_2 x and b = log_3 y. Since x > 1 and y > 1, we have a > 0 and b > 0, with x = 2^a and y = 3^b.
S2. [symbolic] Substitute a and b into the given equation -> {{(log_2 x)^4 + (log_3 y)^4 + 8 = 8(log_2 x)(log_3 y) => a^4 + b^4 + 8 = 8ab}}
S3. [theorem] By AM-GM applied to the four nonnegative terms a^4, b^4, 4, 4, we have a^4 + b^4 + 8 >= 4(a^4 b^4 * 4 * 4)^{1/4} = 8ab.
S4. [derive] The given equation is exactly the equality case of this AM-GM inequality, so equality must hold.
S5. [theorem] Equality in AM-GM for these four terms requires a^4 = b^4 = 4.
S6. [symbolic] Since a > 0 and b > 0, equality gives -> {{a^4 = b^4 = 4 => a = b = sqrt{2}}}
S7. [calc] Compute x^{sqrt{2}} + y^{sqrt{2}} using x = 2^{sqrt{2}} and y = 3^{sqrt{2}} -> <<(2^{sqrt{2}})^{sqrt{2}}+(3^{sqrt{2}})^{sqrt{2}}=13>>

[Check]
V1. Substitute a = b = sqrt{2} into the transformed equation -> <<(sqrt{2})^4+(sqrt{2})^4+8=16>>
V2. Check the right side of the transformed equation -> <<8(sqrt{2})(sqrt{2})=16>>
V3. Check the final exponent simplification -> <<2^{sqrt{2}*sqrt{2}}+3^{sqrt{2}*sqrt{2}}=4+9=13>>

[Answer]
\boxed{13}

[Overview]
This is a cubic equation problem with real coefficients and one nonreal root. The goal is to find a + b. The key idea is that the conjugate of the given root is also a root, and the third root can be found using the sum of the roots.

[Plan]
P1. Use the real coefficients to identify the conjugate root.
P2. Use the sum of the roots to determine the third root.
P3. Multiply the three linear factors to obtain the cubic polynomial.
P4. Read off a and b, then add them.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let z = 1 + i sqrt(3) be a root. Since a and b are real, the coefficients are real, so the conjugate 1 - i sqrt(3) is also a root.
S2. [theorem] For a cubic x^3 + ax + b, the sum of its three roots is 0 because the coefficient of x^2 is 0.
S3. [symbolic] Let r be the third root. The sum of roots is {{(1+i sqrt(3)) + (1-i sqrt(3)) + r = 0 => r = -2}}.
S4. [symbolic] Multiply the corresponding linear factors: {{(x-(1+i sqrt(3)))(x-(1-i sqrt(3)))(x+2) => x^3 + 8}}.
S5. [setup] Comparing x^3 + 8 with x^3 + ax + b gives a = 0 and b = 8.
S6. [calc] Therefore a + b = <<0 + 8 = 8>>.

[Check]
V1. Substitute the given root into x^3 + 8: <<(1+i sqrt(3))^3 + 8 = 0>>.
V2. Expanding the product of the factors gives x^3 + 8, so the coefficients a = 0 and b = 8 are correct.

[Answer]
\boxed{8}

This is a locus problem involving circles and distances. The goal is to find the equation satisfied by the centers of circles externally tangent to C1 and internally tangent to C2. The key idea is to rewrite tangency in terms of distances from the variable center to the two fixed centers, obtaining an ellipse.

[Plan]
P1. Let the variable circle have center (a,b) and radius r.
P2. Translate external tangency to C1 into a distance equation.
P3. Translate internal tangency to C2 into a distance equation.
P4. Eliminate r and identify the resulting locus as an ellipse.
P5. Convert the ellipse equation to the required integer polynomial form.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let the variable circle have center P=(a,b) and radius r, with r>0. The fixed circle C1 has center (0,0) and radius 1. The fixed circle C2 has center (2,0) and radius 4.

S2. [derive] Since the variable circle is externally tangent to C1, its center satisfies sqrt(a^2+b^2)=r+1.

S3. [derive] Since the variable circle is internally tangent to C2, its center satisfies sqrt((a-2)^2+b^2)=4-r.

S4. [symbolic] Add the two distance equations to eliminate r -> {{sqrt(a^2+b^2)+sqrt((a-2)^2+b^2)=(r+1)+(4-r) => sqrt(a^2+b^2)+sqrt((a-2)^2+b^2)=5}}.

S5. [theorem] The locus of points whose distances to the two foci (0,0) and (2,0) have sum 5 is an ellipse.

S6. [derive] The major axis length is 5, so the semi-major axis is A=5/2. The distance between foci is 2, so c=1. Thus the semi-minor axis satisfies B^2=A^2-c^2=25/4-1=21/4, and the center is (1,0).

S7. [symbolic] Write and simplify the ellipse equation -> {{((a-1)^2)/(25/4)+b^2/(21/4)=1 => 84a^2+100b^2-168a-441=0}}.

[Check]
V1. Check the right endpoint (a,b)=(7/2,0): the distance to (0,0) is 7/2, so r=5/2; the distance to (2,0) is 3/2=4-5/2, so the tangency conditions hold.
V2. The final equation is equivalent to 84(a-1)^2+100b^2=525, an ellipse with center (1,0), and the coefficient gcd is 1.

[Answer]
\boxed{84a^2+100b^2-168a-441=0}

sum_k (2a_k - 1)/(a_k^2 - a_k + 1)

The key idea is to use generalized eigenvalues, since the extrema of the quotient of two positive definite quadratic forms occur at values t satisfying det(B - tA) = 0.

[Plan]
P1. Write both quadratic forms using symmetric matrices A and B.
P2. Apply the Lagrange multiplier condition for an extremum subject to the constraint.

P4. Solve the generalized eigenvalue equation det(B - tA) = 0.

S6. [calc] The minimum is m = (3 - sqrt(2))/4 and the maximum is M = (3 + sqrt(2))/4, so their product is -> <<((3-sqrt(2))/4)*((3+sqrt(2))/4)=7/16>>

P2. Use the excluded endpoint of the unbounded interval to identify c.
P3. Use the included endpoints of the bounded interval to identify a and b.
P4. Compute the required expression a + 2b + 3c.
P5. Verify the sign pattern against the original inequality.

S1. [setup] The condition |x - 25| <= 1 is equivalent to 24 <= x <= 26, so the solution set is (-infinity, -4) union [24, 26].

S2. [derive] For R(x) = ((x-a)(x-b))/(x-c), the sign can change only at numerator zeros a, b and at the excluded pole c. Since the solution set is true for x < -4 and excludes x = -4, the point x = -4 must be the excluded pole. Hence c = -4.

S3. [derive] The bounded solution interval is [24, 26], with both endpoints included. These endpoints must be the numerator zeros because the inequality is non-strict and the expression is zero there. Thus {a, b} = {24, 26}. Since a < b, we have a = 24 and b = 26.

S4. [calc] Compute a + 2b + 3c -> <<24 + 2*26 + 3*(-4) = 64>>.

S5. [theorem] The sign of a rational expression changes at simple numerator zeros and at its vertical asymptote, so the intervals determined by -4, 24, and 26 give the complete sign pattern.

[Check]
V1. Substitute a = 24, b = 26, c = -4: R(x) = ((x-24)(x-26))/(x+4).
V2. For x < -4, the numerator is positive and the denominator is negative, so R(x) < 0.
V3. For -4 < x < 24, both numerator and denominator are positive, so R(x) > 0.
V4. For 24 <= x <= 26, the numerator is nonpositive and the denominator is positive, so R(x) <= 0.
V5. For x > 26, both numerator and denominator are positive, so R(x) > 0. Thus the solution set is exactly (-infinity, -4) union [24, 26].

[Answer]

P1. Expand (a + bi)^3 and separate its real and imaginary parts.
P2. Use the condition that the final number is real to set the imaginary part after subtracting 107i equal to zero.
P3. Use divisibility from the resulting integer equation to restrict possible values of b.
P4. Check the possible positive integer cases for a and b.
P5. Compute the corresponding real value and verify it by substitution.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let z = a + bi with a,b positive integers. Expanding gives z^3 = (a^3 - 3ab^2) + i(3a^2b - b^3).
S2. [setup] After subtracting 107i, the imaginary part must be zero, so b(3a^2 - b^2) - 107 = 0, or b(3a^2 - b^2) = 107.
S3. [theorem] Since 107 is prime and b is a positive integer divisor of 107, the only possible positive values are b = 1 or b = 107.
S4. [case] If b = 1, then 3a^2 - 1 = 107, so 3a^2 = 108.
S5. [calc] Solving for a gives <<108/3=36>>, hence a = 6 because a is positive.
S6. [calc] The real part for a = 6 and b = 1 is <<6^3-3*6*1^2=198>>.
S7. [case] If b = 107, then 3a^2 - 107^2 = 1, so 3a^2 = 11450.
S8. [calc] But <<11450/3=11450/3>> is not an integer, contradicting that a is an integer.
S9. [derive] Therefore the only possible positive integer pair is (a,b) = (6,1), giving the real number 198.

[Check]
V1. Substitute a = 6 and b = 1 into the original expression: (6+i)^3 - 107i = 198 + 107i - 107i = 198.
V2. The imaginary part is zero, so the expression is indeed real.
V3. The value is positive and arises from positive integers a,b as required.

[Answer]
\boxed{198}

[Overview]
This is a rational function problem about vertical asymptotes. The goal is to find all constants c for which the graph has exactly one vertical asymptote. The key idea is that vertical asymptotes come from zeros of the denominator after any common factors with the numerator are canceled.

[Plan]
P1. Factor the denominator to locate its zeros.
P2. Determine when the numerator shares a factor with the denominator.
P3. Analyze how cancellation affects the number of remaining vertical asymptotes.
P4. Verify the resulting c-values by factoring the rational function.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Vertical asymptotes can occur where the denominator is zero, unless the numerator also vanishes at the same x-value and cancels the factor.
S2. [symbolic] Factor the denominator -> {{x^2 + x - 20 => (x + 5)(x - 4)}}
S3. [derive] The denominator has zeros x = -5 and x = 4. Normally these give two vertical asymptotes, unless cancellation removes one or both.
S4. [symbolic] Evaluate the numerator at x = -5 -> {{(-5)^2 - (-5) + c => c + 30}}
S5. [symbolic] Evaluate the numerator at x = 4 -> {{4^2 - 4 + c => c + 12}}
S6. [case] If c = -30, the numerator vanishes at x = -5, so the factor x + 5 cancels and only x = 4 remains as a vertical asymptote.
S7. [case] If c = -12, the numerator vanishes at x = 4, so the factor x - 4 cancels and only x = -5 remains as a vertical asymptote.
S8. [case] If neither c + 30 = 0 nor c + 12 = 0, then neither denominator factor cancels, so there are two vertical asymptotes.
S9. [derive] The two numbers c = -30 and c = -12 cannot both occur simultaneously, so they are the only possibilities for exactly one vertical asymptote.

[Check]
V1. For c = -30, f(x) = (x - 6)(x + 5) / ((x + 5)(x - 4)) = (x - 6)/(x - 4) with a hole at x = -5, leaving one vertical asymptote at x = 4.
V2. For c = -12, f(x) = (x - 4)(x + 3) / ((x + 5)(x - 4)) = (x + 3)/(x + 5) with a hole at x = 4, leaving one vertical asymptote at x = -5.
V3. For any other c, neither factor cancels, so both x = -5 and x = 4 are vertical asymptotes.

[Answer]
\boxed{-30,-12}

[Overview]
This is a recurrence relation problem. The goal is to find \(1/a_{2012}+1/b_{2012}\). The key idea is to study the sum and product of \(a_n\) and \(b_n\), since the recurrence gives simple doubling relations for both.

[Plan]
P1. Define the sum \(a_n+b_n\) and product \(a_n b_n\).
P2. Derive how the sum changes from one step to the next.
P3. Derive how the product changes from one step to the next.
P4. Compute the sum and product at \(n=2012\).
P5. Use the reciprocal identity to find the required value.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let \(c_n=a_n+b_n\), \(p_n=a_n b_n\), and \(r_n=\sqrt{a_n^2+b_n^2}\).
S2. [derive] Compute the new sum:
\[
a_{n+1}+b_{n+1}=(a_n+b_n+r_n)+(a_n+b_n-r_n)=2(a_n+b_n),
\]
so \(c_{n+1}=2c_n\).
S3. [derive] Compute the new product:
\[
a_{n+1}b_{n+1}=(a_n+b_n+r_n)(a_n+b_n-r_n)=(a_n+b_n)^2-r_n^2=2a_nb_n,
\]
so \(p_{n+1}=2p_n\).
S4. [calc] Since \(c_0=a_0+b_0=-2+1=-1\) and the sum doubles each step,
\[
c_{2012}=(-1)2^{2012}.
\]
<<c_2012 = (-1)*2^2012 = -2^2012>>
S5. [calc] Since \(p_0=a_0b_0=(-2)(1)=-2\) and the product doubles each step,
\[
p_{2012}=(-2)2^{2012}=-2^{2013}.
\]
<<p_2012 = (-2)*2^2012 = -2^2013>>
S6. [symbolic] Use the reciprocal identity
\[
\frac1{a_n}+\frac1{b_n}=\frac{a_n+b_n}{a_nb_n}=\frac{c_n}{p_n}.
\]
{{1/a_n + 1/b_n = (a_n+b_n)/(a_n b_n) = c_n/p_n}}
S7. [calc] Substitute \(n=2012\):
\[
\frac1{a_{2012}}+\frac1{b_{2012}}=\frac{c_{2012}}{p_{2012}}
=\frac{-2^{2012}}{-2^{2013}}=\frac12.
\]
<<c_2012/p_2012 = (-2^2012)/(-2^2013) = 1/2>>

[Check]
V1. For \(n=0\), the formula gives \(1/a_0+1/b_0=1/(-2)+1/1=1/2\), agreeing with \(\frac{c_0}{p_0}=(-1)/(-2)=1/2\).
V2. The product \(p_n\) is never zero, so the reciprocal expression is valid for all \(n\), including \(n=2012\).

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{1}{2}}

P2. Clear the denominator from both inequalities.
P3. Solve the resulting lower-bound inequality.
P4. Solve the resulting upper-bound inequality.
P5. Intersect the two solution sets and exclude any boundary values.

[Solution]
S1. [symbolic] Complete the square for the denominator -> {{x^2 - 2x + 3 = (x - 1)^2 + 2}}
S2. [theorem] Since (x - 1)^2 + 2 > 0 for every real x, the denominator is positive, so multiplication by it preserves inequality direction.
S3. [symbolic] The left inequality is equivalent to numerator plus denominator being positive -> {{-1 < (x^2 - 14x + 11)/(x^2 - 2x + 3) => 0 < 2x^2 - 16x + 14}}

S5. [derive] A sign analysis gives the left inequality solution x < 1 or x > 7.
S6. [symbolic] The right inequality is equivalent to numerator less than denominator -> {{(x^2 - 14x + 11)/(x^2 - 2x + 3) < 1 => -12x + 8 < 0}}
S7. [derive] Solving -12x + 8 < 0 gives x > 2/3.

[Plan]
P1. Substitute y = x^5 to rewrite the expression as y^2 + y + 1.
P2. Relate y^2 + y + 1 to the factorization of y^3 - 1.
P3. Convert back to x using x^15 - 1 and x^5 - 1.
P4. Identify the two cyclotomic factors over the integers.
P5. State the resulting integer polynomial factorization.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let y = x^5. Then the expression becomes x^10 + x^5 + 1 = y^2 + y + 1.
S2. [theorem] Use the identity y^3 - 1 = (y - 1)(y^2 + y + 1), so y^2 + y + 1 = (y^3 - 1)/(y - 1).
S3. [symbolic] Substitute y = x^5 -> {{(x^5)^2 + x^5 + 1 => (x^15 - 1)/(x^5 - 1)}}
S4. [theorem] Factor x^15 - 1 and x^5 - 1 using cyclotomic polynomials:
x^15 - 1 = Phi_1(x) Phi_3(x) Phi_5(x) Phi_15(x), and x^5 - 1 = Phi_1(x) Phi_5(x).
S5. [symbolic] Cancel the common factors -> {{(Phi_1(x) Phi_3(x) Phi_5(x) Phi_15(x))/(Phi_1(x) Phi_5(x)) => Phi_3(x) Phi_15(x)}}
S6. [symbolic] Substitute the known cyclotomic polynomials -> {{Phi_3(x) Phi_15(x) => (x^2 + x + 1)(x^8 - x^7 + x^5 - x^4 + x^3 - x + 1)}}
S7. [symbolic] Therefore, the original polynomial factors as -> {{x^10 + x^5 + 1 => (x^2 + x + 1)(x^8 - x^7 + x^5 - x^4 + x^3 - x + 1)}}

[Check]

V2. Expand and collect like terms; all intermediate powers cancel, leaving x^10 + x^5 + 1.
V3. Both factors have integer coefficients, as required.

[Answer]
\boxed{(x^2+x+1)(x^8-x^7+x^5-x^4+x^3-x+1)}

solution:
[Overview]
This is a functional equation problem. The goal is to count all functions f : R -> R satisfying f(x + f(y)) = x + y. The key idea is to use x = 0 to show f is an involution, then compare the equation for arbitrary x to force f(y) - y to be constant.

[Plan]
P1. Substitute x = 0 to obtain an involution relation for f.
P2. Use the involution relation to show f is bijective.
P3. Rewrite the original equation with a new variable and show y - f(y) is constant.
P4. Use the involution relation again to determine that constant.
P5. Verify the resulting function and count the solutions.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Write the original equation as f(x + f(y)) = x + y for all real x, y.
S2. [derive] Substitute x = 0 to get f(f(y)) = y for all y, so f composed with itself is the identity.
S3. [theorem] A function with f composed with itself equal to the identity is bijective and is its own inverse.
S4. [derive] Put t = x + f(y). Since x is arbitrary, t is arbitrary for fixed y, and the equation becomes f(t) = t + y - f(y).
S5. [derive] Rearranging gives f(t) - t = y - f(y). The left side depends only on t, while the right side depends only on y, so y - f(y) is a constant c.
S6. [derive] Thus f(y) = y - c for all y.
S7. [derive] Apply f to itself: f(f(y)) = f(y - c) = (y - c) - c = y - 2c. Since f(f(y)) = y, we get y - 2c = y, so c = 0.
S8. [derive] Therefore f(y) = y for all real y. This is the identity function.
S9. [theorem] A function satisfying the equation must be the identity function, so there is exactly one such function.

[Check]
V1. Substitute f(y) = y into the original equation: f(x + f(y)) = f(x + y) = x + y, matching the right side.
V2. The derivation showed c = 0 is forced, so no other linear function f(y) = y - c works.

[Answer]
\boxed{1}

This is a trigonometric optimization problem. The goal is to find the maximum value of a cos(theta) + b sin(theta) for real a and b as theta varies. The key idea is to rewrite the expression as a single cosine wave using a right-triangle normalization.

[Plan]
P1. Define the quantity R = sqrt(a^2 + b^2).
P2. Handle the special case R = 0.
P3. For R > 0, normalize a and b to define an angle phi.
P4. Rewrite the expression using the cosine subtraction identity.
P5. Bound the cosine term by 1 and identify the equality case.
P6. Verify the maximum by substitution.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let R = sqrt(a^2 + b^2). The expression to maximize is E(theta) = a cos(theta) + b sin(theta).
S2. [case] If R = 0, then a = 0 and b = 0, so E(theta) = 0 for all theta, and the maximum is 0.
S3. [setup] Now assume R > 0. Define an angle phi by cos(phi) = a/R and sin(phi) = b/R.
S4. [derive] Using the cosine subtraction identity, E(theta) = R(cos(phi)cos(theta) + sin(phi)sin(theta)) = R cos(theta - phi).
S5. [theorem] For every real x, cos(x) <= 1, so R cos(theta - phi) <= R when R > 0.
S6. [derive] Equality occurs when cos(theta - phi) = 1, for example at theta = phi. Thus the maximum is R = sqrt(a^2 + b^2).
S7. [case] The formula also gives 0 when a = b = 0, so it covers all real a and b.

[Check]
V1. Substitute theta = phi to get a(a/R) + b(b/R) = (a^2 + b^2)/R = R.
V2. Cauchy-Schwarz gives (a cos(theta) + b sin(theta))^2 <= (a^2 + b^2)(cos^2(theta) + sin^2(theta)) = a^2 + b^2, so the value cannot exceed sqrt(a^2 + b^2).
V3. If a = b = 0, then the formula gives 0, which matches the constant zero expression.

[Answer]

[Overview]
This is a number theory problem about the quartic expression x^4 + a^2. The goal is the smallest positive integer a such that x^4 + a^2 is never prime for integer x. The key idea is the Sophie Germain factorization, which shows that a=8 works, and explicit prime witnesses show every smaller a fails.

[Plan]
P1. State the Sophie Germain factorization for x^4 + 4y^4.
P2. Use y=2 to prove that a=8 makes x^4 + a^2 composite for every integer x.
P3. For each a=1 through 7, exhibit an integer x for which x^4 + a^2 is prime.
P4. Conclude that the smallest such positive integer is 8.

[Solution]
S1. [theorem] Use the Sophie Germain identity x^4 + 4y^4 = (x^2 - 2xy + 2y^2)(x^2 + 2xy + 2y^2).
S2. [symbolic] Set y=2, so a=2y^2=8, and factor -> {{x^4+64 = (x^2-4x+8)(x^2+4x+8)}}.
S3. [derive] For every integer x, x^2-4x+8 = (x-2)^2+4 >= 4 and x^2+4x+8 = (x+2)^2+4 >= 4, so both factors are integers greater than 1. Hence x^4+64 is composite for every integer x.
S4. [case] For a=1,2,3,4,5,6,7, the property fails because the following prime values occur:
a=1 with x=1 gives 1^4 + 1^2 = 2, prime.
a=2 with x=1 gives 1^4 + 2^2 = 5, prime.
a=3 with x=10 gives 10^4 + 3^2 = 10009, prime by trial division up to sqrt(10009).
a=4 with x=1 gives 1^4 + 4^2 = 17, prime.
a=5 with x=2 gives 2^4 + 5^2 = 41, prime.
a=6 with x=1 gives 1^4 + 6^2 = 37, prime.
a=7 with x=20 gives 20^4 + 7^2 = 160049, prime by trial division up to sqrt(160049).
S5. [derive] Therefore no positive integer a<8 has the required property, while a=8 does, so the minimum is 8.

[Check]
V1. For a=8, the factorization gives x^4+64 = (x^2-4x+8)(x^2+4x+8), and both factors are always at least 4, so the value is always composite.
V2. For each a<8, the listed x gives a prime value, so each smaller a fails.
V3. Since a=8 works and all smaller positive integers fail, the result is confirmed.

[Answer]
\boxed{8}

[Overview]
This is a piecewise-linear max function problem. The goal is to find the sum of the three x-coordinates where a quadratic polynomial is tangent to the graph. The key idea is to split f into its three linear pieces, impose tangency on each piece, and use the resulting coefficient equations to find the x-coordinates.

[Plan]
P1. Identify the three linear pieces and the intervals where each is active.
P2. Let the quadratic have leading coefficient a and let x1, x2, x3 be its tangency points on the three pieces.
P3. Use the double-root condition for the difference between the quadratic and each linear piece.
P4. Compare coefficients between adjacent pieces to derive equations for x1, x2, x3.
P5. Solve those equations and verify the points lie in the correct intervals.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Write the three linear functions as L1(x) = -11x - 37, L2(x) = x - 1, and L3(x) = 9x + 3, and let p(x) = ax^2 + bx + c with a not equal to 0.

S2. [derive] Compare the linear pieces to determine f: L1 is active for x <= -3, L2 is active for -3 <= x <= -1/2, and L3 is active for x >= -1/2.

S3. [theorem] A nonzero quadratic cannot be tangent to the same line at two distinct points, since the difference would be a quadratic with two double roots. Thus the three tangency points lie one on each active linear piece.

S4. [setup] Let x1 be on L1, x2 be on L2, and x3 be on L3. At each tangency point, p(x) - Li(x) has a double root at xi, so p(x) = Li(x) + a(x - xi)^2 for i = 1, 2, 3.

S5. [derive] Equating p(x) = L1(x) + a(x - x1)^2 and p(x) = L2(x) + a(x - x2)^2 gives a(x2 - x1) = 6 and x1 + x2 = -6.

S6. [derive] Equating p(x) = L2(x) + a(x - x2)^2 and p(x) = L3(x) + a(x - x3)^2 gives a(x3 - x2) = 4 and x2 + x3 = -1.

S7. [derive] Let y = x2. Then x1 = -6 - y and x3 = -1 - y. Also x2 - x1 = 2y + 6 and x3 - x2 = -1 - 2y, so a(2y + 6) = 6 and a(-1 - 2y) = 4.

S8. [symbolic] Divide the two equations to eliminate a -> {{(2*y+6)/(-1-2*y)=3/2 => y=-3/2}}

S9. [calc] Substitute y = -3/2 to get x1 = -9/2, x2 = -3/2, and x3 = 1/2, so the desired sum is -> <<(-9/2)+(-3/2)+(1/2)=-11/2>>

[Check]
V1. The points satisfy the active intervals: x1 = -9/2 <= -3, x2 = -3/2 is in [-3, -1/2], and x3 = 1/2 >= -1/2.
V2. The corresponding quadratic is p(x) = 2x^2 + 7x + 7/2, with p'(x) = 4x + 7.
V3. At x1, x2, x3, the slopes of p are -11, 1, 9, matching L1, L2, L3 respectively, and the values also match at those points.

[Answer]
\boxed{-11/2}

This is an infinite series problem with alternating denominator patterns. The goal is to express the sum as a reduced fraction a/b and compute a+b. The key idea is to split the series into odd-indexed and even-indexed terms, then evaluate each using geometric-series derivative formulas.

[Plan]
P1. Separate the series into odd-indexed terms with denominator powers of 2 and even-indexed terms with denominator powers of 3.
P2. Reindex each part as a power series in 1/4 or 1/9.
P3. Use the geometric-series derivative formula to evaluate both sums.
P4. Add the rational results, reduce a/b, and compute a+b.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let S be the given sum and split it as S = S_odd + S_even, where S_odd = sum_{k=1}^{infty} (2k-1)/2^{2k-1} and S_even = sum_{k=1}^{infty} (2k)/3^{2k}.
S2. [theorem] For |r|<1, sum_{k=1}^{infty} k r^k = r/(1-r)^2 and sum_{k=0}^{infty} r^k = 1/(1-r).
S3. [derive] Reindex the odd part by writing 2^{2k-1}=2*4^{k-1}; then S_odd = (1/2) sum_{j=0}^{infty} (2j+1)(1/4)^j.
S4. [calc] Evaluate the even part -> <<2*(1/9)/(1-1/9)^2=9/32>>
S5. [calc] Evaluate the odd part -> <<(1/2)*(2*(1/4)/(1-1/4)^2+1/(1-1/4))=10/9>>
S6. [calc] Add the two parts -> <<10/9+9/32=401/288>>
S7. [calc] Since 401 and 288 are relatively prime, compute a+b -> <<401+288=689>>

V2. The fraction 401/288 is about 1.392, which is reasonable because the positive series is slightly larger than the odd-part sum 10/9.

[Answer]
\boxed{689}

[Overview]
This is a polynomial interpolation and summation problem. The goal is to find the sum of a cubic polynomial p(x) from x=1 to x=21 using four known values. The key idea is to shift the variable by 11, use symmetry in the given points, and sum over a symmetric interval.

[Plan]
P1. Shift the variable by setting y=x-11 so the given x-values become symmetric.
P2. Write the shifted cubic q(y)=p(y+11).
P3. Use paired values of q to determine its even and constant parts.
P4. Sum p(x) from x=1 to x=21 over the symmetric y-values.
P5. Verify the symmetry and summation logic.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let q(y)=p(y+11), so p(x)=q(x-11). The given values become q(-9)=1, q(-4)=19, q(4)=11, and q(9)=29.
S2. [setup] Since p is cubic, write q(y)=A y^3+B y^2+C y+D.
S3. [derive] Compute q(9)-q(-9): 1458A+18C=28.
S4. [derive] Compute q(4)-q(-4): 128A+8C=-8.
S5. [derive] Compute q(9)+q(-9): 162B+2D=30.
S6. [derive] Compute q(4)+q(-4): 32B+2D=30.
S7. [derive] Subtract the two sum equations to get 130B=0, so B=0. Wait, division check: (162B+2D)-(32B+2D)=130B, but the right sides are both 30, so 130B=0.

Correction: using divided forms gives 81B+D=15 and 16B+D=15, so 65B=0. Thus B=0.

S8. [derive] With B=0, the equation 16B+D=15 gives D=15. Therefore q(y)=A y^3+C y+15, so p(x)=A(x-11)^3+C(x-11)+15.
S9. [derive] As x runs from 1 to 21, y=x-11 runs from -10 to 10. The sums of y and y^3 over this symmetric interval are both 0.
S10. [calc] Thus the requested sum is 21 copies of 15 -> <<21*15=315>>.

[Check]
V1. The paired values satisfy q(9)+q(-9)=29+1=30 and q(4)+q(-4)=11+19=30, which is consistent with B=0 and D=15.
V2. The summation interval y=-10 to 10 has 21 terms and is symmetric, so all odd-power terms cancel, leaving only 21*15=315.

[Answer]

[Overview]
This is a telescoping sum problem involving square roots. The goal is to compute the floor of S^2, where S is a finite sum of radical terms. The key idea is to simplify each radical into a telescoping expression.

[Plan]
P1. Express the general radical term in a simpler algebraic form.
P2. Simplify the radical using a perfect square.
P3. Sum the resulting telescoping series from 1 to 2007.
P4. Square the total and determine its floor.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] For k = 1, 2, ..., 2007, let a_k = sqrt(1 + 1/k^2 + 1/(k+1)^2), so S = sum_{k=1}^{2007} a_k.
S2. [symbolic] Combine the terms under the radical -> {{1 + 1/k^2 + 1/(k+1)^2 => (k^2+k+1)^2/[k^2(k+1)^2]}}
S3. [symbolic] Simplify the radical using the positive square root -> {{sqrt((k^2+k+1)^2/[k^2(k+1)^2]) => (k^2+k+1)/(k(k+1))}}
S4. [symbolic] Rewrite the term as a telescoping difference -> {{(k^2+k+1)/(k(k+1)) => 1 + 1/k - 1/(k+1)}}
S5. [theorem] The sum of the telescoping part is sum_{k=1}^{2007}(1/k - 1/(k+1)) = 1 - 1/2008.
S6. [calc] Add the constant 1 from each of the 2007 terms -> <<2007 + (1 - 1/2008)=2008 - 1/2008>>
S7. [calc] Square S -> <<(2008 - 1/2008)^2=4032062 + 1/4032064>>
S8. [calc] Take the floor, using 0 < 1/4032064 < 1 -> <<floor(4032062 + 1/4032064)=4032062>>

[Check]
V1. For k = 1, the formula gives sqrt(1 + 1 + 1/4) = 3/2, matching 1 + 1 - 1/2 = 3/2.
V2. Since S = 2008 - 1/2008, we have S^2 = 4032062 + 1/4032064, which lies strictly between 4032062 and 4032063, so its floor is 4032062.

[Overview]
This is a probability problem involving a real parameter b and the number of real solutions of an even quartic equation. The goal is the probability that the equation has at least two distinct real solutions. The key idea is to set y=x^2, reducing the quartic to a quadratic in y whose positive roots correspond to real x solutions.

[Plan]
P1. Set y=x^2 and rewrite the original equation as a quadratic in y.
P2. Relate distinct real x solutions to positive real roots y.
P3. Derive the conditions on b for the quadratic in y to have a positive real root.
P4. Determine the total length of b-values in [-17,17] satisfying the condition.
P5. Compute the reduced probability and then m+n.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let y=x^2 with y>=0. The equation becomes y^2-(4b^2-10b)y+25b^2=0.
S2. [derive] For y>0, each positive root gives two distinct real x values, x=sqrt(y) and x=-sqrt(y). A root y=0 gives only x=0, so at least two distinct real x solutions occur exactly when the y-quadratic has at least one positive real root.
S3. [symbolic] Let A=4b^2-10b. The discriminant in y is A^2-100b^2 -> {{(4b^2-10b)^2-100b^2 => 16b^3(b-5)}}.
S4. [derive] Real y roots require 16b^3(b-5)>=0. On [-17,17], this gives b in [-17,0] union [5,17].
S5. [derive] For b=0, the only y root is y=0, so there is only x=0 and b=0 does not qualify. For b<0 or b>=5, the product of the y roots is 25b^2>0 and their sum A=4b^2-10b is positive, so the real roots are positive, or positive double at b=5.
S6. [calc] Total length of qualifying b-values is (0-(-17))+(17-5) -> <<17+12=29>>.
S7. [calc] The total interval length is 17-(-17) -> <<17+17=34>>.
S8. [calc] The reduced probability is 29/34, so m+n=29+34 -> <<29+34=63>>.

[Check]
V1. For b=-1, the discriminant is 16*(-1)^3*(-1-5), which is positive, and A=14>0, so positive y roots exist.
V2. For b=1, the discriminant is 16*1^3*(1-5), which is negative, so there are no real y roots and no real x solutions.
V3. The probability 29/34 is between 0 and 1, and the qualifying intervals have total length 29 out of 34.

[Answer]
\boxed{63}

[Overview]
This is a sequence-block problem. The goal is to find the 2008th term of a sequence constructed in blocks of increasing length and changing congruence modulo 3. The key idea is to locate the block containing the 2008th term using triangular numbers, then compute the term from the block's starting value and common difference.

[Plan]
P1. Express the total number of terms through block n as a triangular number.
P2. Locate the block containing u_2008.
P3. Derive a formula for the last term of each block.
P4. Find the first term and the desired position within the located block.
P5. Compute the required term and verify it.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let block n contain n terms, all congruent to n modulo 3. Let L_n be the last term of block n, and set L_0 = 0.
S2. [derive] Since L_{n-1} is congruent to n-1 modulo 3, the smallest integer greater than L_{n-1} that is congruent to n modulo 3 is L_{n-1}+1. Thus the first term of block n is L_{n-1}+1.
S3. [symbolic] Block n increases by 3 each term, so {{L_n = L_{n-1} + 1 + 3(n-1) => L_n = L_{n-1} + 3n - 2}}.
S4. [symbolic] Summing the recurrence from k = 1 to n gives {{L_n = \sum_{k=1}^n (3k-2) => L_n = \frac{n(3n-1)}{2}}}.
S5. [calc] Compute the total number of terms through block 62 -> <<T_62 = 62*63/2 = 1953>>.
S6. [calc] Compute the total number of terms through block 63 -> <<T_63 = 63*64/2 = 2016>>.
S7. [derive] Since 1953 < 2008 <= 2016, the term u_2008 lies in block 63.
S8. [calc] Find its position within block 63 -> <<2008 - 1953 = 55>>.
S9. [calc] Compute the last term of block 62 -> <<L_62 = 62*(3*62-1)/2 = 5735>>.
S10. [calc] The first term of block 63 is L_62+1, so the 55th term is -> <<5736 + 3*(55-1) = 5898>>.

[Check]
V1. The cumulative term counts T_62 = 1953 and T_63 = 2016 place the 2008th term at position 55 in block 63.
V2. The first term of block 63 is 5735+1 = 5736, and its terms increase by 3.
V3. The 55th term is 5736 + 3*54 = 5898, and reversing gives (5898-5736)/3 + 1 = 55, as required.

[Answer]
\boxed{5898}

[Overview]
This is a polynomial roots and Vieta problem. The goal is to find the greatest lower bound of the sum of squares of the roots under the coefficient relation \(a_{n-1}=-a_{n-2}\), and then take its absolute value. The key idea is to express the sum of squares using Vieta's formulas as a quadratic in \(a_{n-1}\) and minimize it.

[Plan]
P1. Let the roots be \(r_1,\dots,r_n\) and express the given coefficients using \(t=a_{n-1}\).
P2. Use Vieta's formulas for the sum and pairwise sum of the roots.
P3. Write the sum of squares of the roots in terms of \(t\).
P4. Complete the square to find the greatest lower bound.
P5. Verify that the lower bound is attainable and take its absolute value.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let \(P(x)=x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+a_{n-2}x^{n-2}+\cdots\) with roots \(r_1,\dots,r_n\), and set \(t=a_{n-1}\). Since \(a_{n-1}=-a_{n-2}\), we have \(a_{n-2}=-t\).
S2. [theorem] By Vieta's formulas, \(\sum_{i=1}^n r_i=-a_{n-1}=-t\) and \(\sum_{1\le i<j\le n} r_i r_j=a_{n-2}=-t\).
S3. [symbolic] The sum of squares of the roots is \(S=\sum r_i^2=(\sum r_i)^2-2\sum_{i<j}r_i r_j\), so {{S = (-t)^2 - 2(-t) => S = t^2 + 2t}}.
S4. [symbolic] Complete the square in \(t\): {{t^2 + 2t => (t+1)^2 - 1}}.
S5. [theorem] Since \((t+1)^2\ge 0\) for real \(t\), we have \(S\ge -1\), with equality when \(t=-1\).
S6. [case] Take \(n=2\) and \(P(x)=x^2-x+1\). Then \(a_1=-1\) and \(a_0=1\), so \(a_1=-a_0\), and the lower bound \(-1\) is attained. Thus the greatest lower bound is \(-1\), whose absolute value is \(1\).

[Check]
V1. For \(P(x)=x^2-x+1\), Vieta gives \(r_1+r_2=1\) and \(r_1r_2=1\), so \(r_1^2+r_2^2=1^2-2\cdot 1= -1\), matching the bound <<1^2-2*1=-1>>.
V2. The expression \(t^2+2t\) has minimum \(-1\) at \(t=-1\), so the computed lower bound is consistent.

[Answer]
\boxed{1}

S2. [derive] Expanding and comparing coefficients gives b=m+n and mn=2008b=2008(m+n).

S6. [calc] Count positive divisors of N -> <<(6+1)(2+1)=21>>
S7. [derive] For d>0, b=4016+d+N/d and d+N/d>=2*2008=4016, so b>=8032. For d<0, write d=-a with a>0; then b=4016-(a+N/a)<=0. Thus the positive and negative divisor cases give disjoint b values.
S8. [derive] For positive divisors, d1+N/d1=d2+N/d2 implies (d1-d2)(1-N/(d1 d2))=0, so the only duplication is d and N/d. The same pairing holds for negative divisors. Hence distinct b values correspond to unordered positive divisor pairs {a,N/a}, giving 4016+(a+N/a) and 4016-(a+N/a).
S9. [calc] Count unordered positive divisor pairs of N -> <<(21+1)/2=11>>
S10. [calc] Sum the two b values for each unordered pair -> <<(4016+(a+N/a))+(4016-(a+N/a))=8032>>
S11. [calc] Sum over all 11 unordered pairs -> <<11*8032=88352>>

S4. [derive] Therefore x_i/(1-x_i^2) >= (3*sqrt(3)/2)x_i^2 for every i.

The key idea is to use the Newton recurrence for the roots and determine all possible quadratic equations from the first few power-sum equalities.

[Plan]
P1. Introduce the power sums a_n and the coefficients s and p.
P2. Use a_1 = a_2 to relate p to s.
P3. Use the recurrence and a_3 = a_1 to determine possible values of s and p.
P4. Exclude cases with a zero root and evaluate the reciprocal sum for the valid case.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let a_n = r1^n + r2^n, s = r1 + r2, and p = r1 r2. Then a_1 = s, and the condition gives a_1 = a_2 = ... = a_2007.
S2. [derive] Since a_2 = r1^2 + r2^2 = s^2 - 2p and a_2 = a_1 = s, we get s^2 - 2p = s, so p = (s^2 - s)/2.
S3. [derive] By the Newton recurrence, a_3 = s a_2 - p a_1 = s^2 - ps = s(s - p). Since a_3 = a_1 = s, we get s(s - p) = s, so s = 0 or s - p = 1.
S4. [case] If s = 0, then p = (0^2 - 0)/2 = 0, so the quadratic is x^2, whose roots are both 0. The reciprocal expression is undefined.
S5. [case] If s != 0, then p = s - 1. Combining with p = (s^2 - s)/2 gives s - 1 = (s^2 - s)/2, so s^2 - 3s + 2 = 0, hence s = 1 or s = 2.
S6. [case] If s = 1, then p = 0, so one root is 0 and the reciprocal expression is undefined. If s = 2, then p = 1, and the roots are both 1.
S7. [calc] For r1 = r2 = 1, the required sum is 1/1^2008 + 1/1^2008 = <<1/1^2008+1/1^2008=2>>.
S8. [theorem] Therefore, among the cases where the reciprocal expression is defined, the only possible roots are both 1, giving the greatest possible value.

[Check]
V1. The roots r1 = r2 = 1 satisfy the quadratic x^2 - 2x + 1 = (x - 1)^2.
V2. For every positive integer k, r1^k + r2^k = 1 + 1 = 2, so the required equal power-sum condition holds through k = 2007.
V3. The reciprocal sum is 1 + 1 = 2, matching the computed maximum.

[Answer]
\boxed{2}

This is a constrained minimization problem for a homogeneous quadratic expression. The goal is to find the smallest possible value of the given ratio. The key idea is to normalize by b, reducing the problem to minimizing a quadratic function of two variables, then checking that its global minimum satisfies b > c > a.

[Plan]
P1. Define normalized variables x = a/b and y = c/b.
P2. Express the target expression as a quadratic in x and y.
P3. Find the unconstrained minimum of this quadratic.
P4. Verify that the minimizing pair can be realized with b > c > a and b not equal to 0.
P5. Conclude the smallest possible value.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let x = a/b and y = c/b. Since b is nonzero, the expression becomes E = (x+1)^2 + (1-y)^2 + (y-x)^2.
S2. [derive] Expanding gives E = 2x^2 + 2y^2 - 2xy + 2x - 2y + 2.
S3. [derive] Setting the partial derivatives to zero gives 2x - y + 1 = 0 and -x + 2y - 1 = 0, whose solution is x = -1/3 and y = 1/3.
S4. [theorem] The Hessian of E is positive definite, so this critical point is the unique global minimum of the quadratic over all real x and y.
S5. [calc] Evaluate E at x = -1/3 and y = 1/3 -> <<2*(-1/3)^2+2*(1/3)^2-2*(-1/3)*(1/3)+2*(-1/3)-2*(1/3)+2=4/3>>
S6. [derive] Taking b = 1, a = -1/3, and c = 1/3 gives b > c > a and b is nonzero, so the global minimum is attainable under the constraints.

[Overview]
This is a prime-value problem for a quartic polynomial. The goal is to find all positive integers n such that f(n) is prime and then sum those prime values. The key idea is to factor f(n) so that primeness forces one factor to equal 1.

[Plan]
P1. Factor the quartic polynomial into two integer factors.
P2. Use the fact that a positive prime has exactly two positive divisors.
P3. Determine which positive integer n can make one factor equal to 1.
P4. Check that the corresponding other factors are prime.
P5. Sum the prime values of f(n).

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let f(n) = n^4 - 360n^2 + 400 and consider positive integer n.
S2. [symbolic] Factor the quartic as a difference of squares -> {{n^4 - 360n^2 + 400 => (n^2 - 20n + 20)(n^2 + 20n + 20)}}
S3. [derive] For positive n, the second factor n^2 + 20n + 20 is positive and greater than 1.
S4. [theorem] A product of two integers greater than 1 is composite, so for f(n) to be prime, the first factor must be 1.
S5. [derive] Solve n^2 - 20n + 20 = 1 by writing n^2 - 20n + 19 = (n - 1)(n - 19) = 0.
S6. [case] The positive integer solutions are n = 1 and n = 19.
S7. [calc] Compute f(1) from the second factor -> <<1^2 + 20*1 + 20 = 41>>
S8. [calc] Compute f(19) from the second factor -> <<19^2 + 20*19 + 20 = 761>>
S9. [derive] Both 41 and 761 are prime; 761 has no prime divisor among 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 23, and its square root is less than 28.
S10. [calc] Add the prime values -> <<41 + 761 = 802>>

[Check]

V2. Substitute n = 19 directly into f(n): <<19^4 - 360*19^2 + 400 = 761>>
V3. Check the sum of the two prime values: <<41 + 761 = 802>>

[Answer]
\boxed{802}

P2. Use symmetry to relate h(a,b) and h(b,a).
P3. Reduce the pair (14,52) using remainders until a divisibility base case appears.
P4. Recover f(14,52) from h(14,52) and verify the result.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Define h(x,y)=f(x,y)/y for positive integers x and y.
S2. [derive] From (x+y)f(x,y)=y f(x,x+y), divide by y(x+y) to get h(x,y)=h(x,x+y). Thus for fixed x, h(x,y) is unchanged when y is increased or decreased by x.
S3. [derive] Since f(x,x)=x, we have h(x,x)=1. By repeated use of S2, h(x,kx)=1 for every positive integer k.
S4. [derive] Symmetry gives f(x,y)=f(y,x), so y h(x,y)=x h(y,x), or h(x,y)=(x/y)h(y,x).
S5. [derive] Since 52=3*14+10, the invariance in S2 gives h(14,52)=h(14,10). Symmetry gives 10h(14,10)=14h(10,14), so h(14,10)=(7/5)h(10,14).
S6. [derive] Since 14=1*10+4, h(10,14)=h(10,4). Symmetry gives 4h(10,4)=10h(4,10), so h(10,4)=(5/2)h(4,10).
S7. [derive] Since 10=2*4+2, h(4,10)=h(4,2). Symmetry gives 2h(4,2)=4h(2,4), so h(4,2)=2h(2,4).
S8. [derive] Because 4 is a multiple of 2, S3 gives h(2,4)=1. Hence h(4,2)=2, h(4,10)=2, h(10,4)=5, h(10,14)=5, h(14,10)=7, and h(14,52)=7.
S9. [calc] Recover the required value from f(14,52)=52h(14,52) -> <<52*7=364>>.

[Overview]
This is a counting problem about integer factorization of monic quadratics. The goal is to count ordered pairs (a,b) with 1 <= a <= 100 and b >= 0 such that x^2+ax+b has an integer linear factorization. The key idea is to write the factorization as (x+c)(x+d), which gives a=c+d and b=cd, then count distinct products for each fixed a.

[Plan]
P1. Translate the integer factorization into equations involving integer c and d.
P2. Use b >= 0 and a > 0 to determine the allowed signs of c and d.
P3. For each fixed a, count how many distinct products cd can occur with c+d=a.
P4. Sum this count over a = 1 to 100.
P5. Verify the fixed-a formula with small cases and check the final sum.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Write x^2+ax+b=(x+c)(x+d) with c and d integers. Expanding gives a=c+d and b=cd.
S2. [derive] Since a>0 and b=cd>=0, c and d must both be nonnegative. If both were negative, their sum would be negative, and if they had opposite signs, their product would be negative.
S3. [derive] For fixed a, each unordered pair {c,d} of nonnegative integers with c+d=a gives one product b=cd. Different unordered pairs give different products because c and d are determined by their sum a and product b.
S4. [derive] The unordered pairs c<=d with c+d=a are obtained by choosing c=0,1,...,floor(a/2). Hence the number of possible b for fixed a is floor(a/2)+1.
S5. [calc] Sum this count over all a from 1 to 100 -> <<sum_{a=1}^{100} (floor(a/2)+1)=2600>>.

[Check]

V2. The sum of floor(a/2) for a=1,...,100 is 2500, so adding 100 gives 2600, matching the calculation.

[Answer]
\boxed{2600}

[Overview]
This is a Diophantine equation problem involving consecutive positive perfect cubes. The goal is to find the smallest possible z such that the sum of the first three consecutive cubes equals the fourth. The key idea is to parameterize the four consecutive perfect cubes by a positive integer n and solve the resulting polynomial equation.

[Plan]
P1. Let the four consecutive positive perfect cubes be expressed using one integer n.
P2. Substitute the first three cubes into the left side and the fourth cube into the right side.
P3. Expand and simplify the resulting equation.
P4. Factor the simplified equation and use positivity to determine n.
P5. Compute z and verify the equality.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let the four distinct consecutive positive perfect cubes in ascending order be n^3, (n+1)^3, (n+2)^3, and (n+3)^3, where n is a positive integer.
S2. [symbolic] Substitute these cubes into the given equation and simplify -> {{n^3+(n+1)^3+(n+2)^3=(n+3)^3 => n^3-6n-9=0}}
S3. [symbolic] Factor the simplified polynomial -> {{n^3-6n-9 => (n-3)(n^2+3n+3)}}
S4. [theorem] For positive n, the factor n^2+3n+3 is positive, so the equation (n-3)(n^2+3n+3)=0 forces n-3=0.
S5. [calc] Solve for n and compute z=n+3 -> <<3+3=6>>
S6. [derive] Since the positive integer n is uniquely forced to be 3, the corresponding value is z=6 and no smaller positive z can work.

[Check]
V1. Substitute n=3 into the original cube sum -> <<3^3+4^3+5^3=216>>
V2. Compare with the fourth cube -> <<6^3=216>>
V3. The cubes 27, 64, 125, and 216 are distinct, consecutive positive perfect cubes in ascending order.

[Overview]
This is a homogeneous quadratic inequality problem over nonnegative variables. The goal is to find the largest real lambda such that the quadratic form is always nonnegative. The key idea is to complete squares in a and d, reducing the problem to a two-variable inequality in b and c.

[Plan]
P1. Rewrite the inequality as a nonnegative quadratic form.
P2. Complete squares in the variables a and d.
P3. Reduce the condition to a quadratic inequality in b and c.
P4. Find the largest lambda for which that reduced inequality always holds.
P5. Verify the critical value and show larger values fail.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Define Q = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + d^2 - ab - lambda bc - cd. We need Q >= 0 for all nonnegative a,b,c,d.
S2. [derive] Complete squares in a and d to get Q = (a - b/2)^2 + (d - c/2)^2 + (3/4)b^2 + (3/4)c^2 - lambda bc.
S3. [theorem] Since the squared terms are nonnegative and can be made zero by choosing a = b/2 and d = c/2, the condition Q >= 0 for all nonnegative variables is equivalent to (3/4)b^2 + (3/4)c^2 - lambda bc >= 0 for all b,c >= 0.
S4. [derive] If bc > 0, divide by bc and set t = b/c > 0. The condition becomes lambda <= (3/4)(t + 1/t). Thus lambda is at most the minimum of (3/4)(t + 1/t) over t > 0.
S5. [calc] The minimum occurs at t = 1, giving <<(3/4)*(1+1)=3/2>>.
S6. [derive] At lambda = 3/2, the reduced expression equals (3/4)(b-c)^2, so Q = (a-b/2)^2 + (d-c/2)^2 + (3/4)(b-c)^2 >= 0.
S7. [case] If lambda > 3/2, choose b = c = 1 and a = d = 1/2. Then Q = 3/2 - lambda < 0, so no larger lambda works.

[Check]
V1. At lambda = 3/2, the completed-square identity gives a sum of squares, so the inequality holds for all nonnegative a,b,c,d.
V2. At b = c = 1 and a = d = 1/2, the value is Q = 3/2 - lambda, which is negative whenever lambda > 3/2.
V3. Therefore 3/2 is both attainable and maximal.

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{3}{2}}

[Overview]
This is a polynomial common-root problem. The goal is to find real coefficients a and b for which the two cubics share two distinct roots. The key idea is to subtract the cubics so that the common roots satisfy a quadratic, then use Vieta relations to determine the common roots and coefficients.

[Plan]
P1. Let the two distinct common roots be r and s, and subtract the two cubics.
P2. Use the resulting quadratic to relate the sum and product of r and s to b-a.
P3. Express the third root of each cubic using the constant term.
P4. Use the x-coefficient of the first cubic to determine the product of the common roots.
P5. Recover the common roots, then compute a and b from root sums.
P6. Verify by substitution into both cubics.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let r and s be two distinct common roots, and let t and u be the third roots of the first and second cubic, respectively.
S2. [derive] Subtracting the first cubic from the second gives (b-a)x^2+3x+2, so r and s are exactly the roots of c x^2+3x+2=0 where c=b-a is nonzero.
S3. [derive] By Vieta for c x^2+3x+2=0, with R=rs and S=r+s, we have cS=-3 and cR=2, hence S=(-3/2)R.
S4. [derive] For the first cubic, the constant term gives rst=-6, so since R=rs is nonzero, t=-6/R.
S5. [derive] The x-coefficient of the first cubic gives R+tS=11. Substituting t=-6/R and S=(-3/2)R gives R+9=11, so R=2.
S6. [derive] Then S=(-3/2)R=-3, so r and s are the roots of x^2-Sx+R=x^2+3x+2=(x+1)(x+2).
S7. [derive] Thus the common roots are -1 and -2. The first cubic has third root t=-6/R=-3, and the second cubic has third root u=-8/R=-4.
S8. [symbolic] Expand the first cubic with roots -1,-2,-3 -> {{(x+1)(x+2)(x+3) => x^3+6x^2+11x+6}}
S9. [symbolic] Expand the second cubic with roots -1,-2,-4 -> {{(x+1)(x+2)(x+4) => x^3+7x^2+14x+8}}
S10. [derive] Comparing coefficients gives a=6 and b=7, so the ordered pair is (6,7).

[Check]
V1. Substitute x=-1 into the first cubic with a=6: <<(-1)^3+6(-1)^2+11(-1)+6=0>>
V2. Substitute x=-2 into the first cubic with a=6: <<(-2)^3+6(-2)^2+11(-2)+6=0>>
V3. Substitute x=-1 into the second cubic with b=7: <<(-1)^3+7(-1)^2+14(-1)+8=0>>
V4. Substitute x=-2 into the second cubic with b=7: <<(-2)^3+7(-2)^2+14(-2)+8=0>>
V5. The numbers -1 and -2 are distinct, so the two common roots requirement is satisfied.

[Answer]
\boxed{(6,7)}

S6. [case] On (-infinity, -7/4), test x = -2: numerator = -1 and denominator = -1, so the quotient is positive.

[Overview]
This is a minimal polynomial problem over the rational numbers. The goal is to find the monic rational-coefficient polynomial of least degree having the two given algebraic numbers as roots. The key idea is that rational coefficients force the conjugate roots, so multiply the minimal quadratic factors.

[Plan]
P1. Identify the minimal polynomial for 1+sqrt(2) over the rationals.
P2. Identify the minimal polynomial for 1+sqrt(3) over the rationals.
P3. Explain why both quadratic conjugate pairs are required.
P4. Multiply the two minimal factors and expand.
P5. Verify the roots, expansion, and minimality.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let a = 1+sqrt(2) and b = 1+sqrt(3). Because the coefficients must be rational, the conjugates 1-sqrt(2) and 1-sqrt(3) must also be roots.
S2. [symbolic] The minimal factor for 1+sqrt(2) is -> {{(x-(1+sqrt(2)))(x-(1-sqrt(2))) => x^2 - 2x - 1}}
S3. [symbolic] The minimal factor for 1+sqrt(3) is -> {{(x-(1+sqrt(3)))(x-(1-sqrt(3))) => x^2 - 2x - 2}}
S4. [theorem] If a polynomial over Q has a quadratic irrational root whose minimal polynomial is quadratic, then it must contain that whole minimal quadratic factor.
S5. [derive] The conjugates 1-sqrt(2) and 1-sqrt(3) are distinct from a and b and from each other, so any rational polynomial containing both a and b must contain four distinct roots. Therefore the minimal degree is at least 4.
S6. [symbolic] Multiply the two minimal quadratic factors -> {{(x^2 - 2x - 1)(x^2 - 2x - 2) => x^4 - 4x^3 + x^2 + 6x + 2}}

[Check]
V1. Since x^2 - 2x - 1 is a factor, substituting x = 1+sqrt(2) gives zero, so 1+sqrt(2) is a root.
V2. Since x^2 - 2x - 2 is a factor, substituting x = 1+sqrt(3) gives zero, so 1+sqrt(3) is a root.
V3. The four roots forced by rational conjugation are distinct, so no rational monic polynomial of degree less than 4 can contain both required roots.

[Answer]
\boxed{x^4 - 4x^3 + x^2 + 6x + 2}

P2. Write the quotient as x+d and expand (x+d)g(x).
P3. Compare coefficients with f(x) to solve for d and a, and for b and c if needed.
P4. Evaluate f(1) using the factorization of f.

S1. [setup] Let the three distinct roots of g be r1, r2, r3. Since each is also a root of f, the cubic g divides the quartic f. Because both are monic, there is a real d with f(x)=(x+d)g(x).

S4. [calc] From the x-coefficient equation, d = <<100-10=90>>.

P1. Determine the domain of the logarithms.

S5. [symbolic] Convert from logarithmic form to exponential form -> {{log_5(x^3-2) = 2 => x^3-2 = 5^2}}
S6. [symbolic] Simplify and solve the resulting cubic -> {{x^3-2 = 5^2 => x^3 = 27}}

[Overview]
This is a number theory problem involving sums of squares and a Pell-type square condition. The goal is the largest n <= 2008 for which the product is a perfect square. The key idea is to simplify the two sums, reduce the square condition to (n+1)(7n+1) being a square, and solve the resulting Pell equation.

[Plan]
P1. Use the sum of squares formula to simplify both factors.
P2. Factor out an already square term from the product.
P3. Reduce the remaining condition to an integer square equation.
P4. Convert this equation to a Pell-type equation.
P5. Generate all admissible solutions up to the bound and choose the largest n.
P6. Verify the chosen value.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let A = 1^2+2^2+...+n^2 and B=(n+1)^2+...+(2n)^2. The required product is P=A B.
S2. [symbolic] Apply the sum of squares formula to the first factor -> {{1^2+2^2+...+n^2 => n(n+1)(2n+1)/6}}
S3. [symbolic] Subtract the first sum from the sum of squares through 2n -> {{(n+1)^2+...+(2n)^2 => n(2n+1)(7n+1)/6}}
S4. [symbolic] Multiply the two simplified factors -> {{[n(n+1)(2n+1)/6][n(2n+1)(7n+1)/6] => [n(2n+1)/6]^2 (n+1)(7n+1)}}
S5. [theorem] The rational factor [n(2n+1)/6]^2 is already a square, so P is a perfect square exactly when (n+1)(7n+1) is a perfect square.
S6. [setup] Write (n+1)(7n+1)=m^2 and set x=7n+4. The restriction n<=2008 becomes x<=14060 and x is 4 mod 7.
S7. [symbolic] Complete the square relation for the square condition -> {{(7n+4)^2 - 7(n+1)(7n+1) => 9}}
S8. [derive] Using x=7n+4 and y=m, the condition becomes the Pell-type equation x^2 - 7 y^2 = 9, with x positive and x mod 7 = 4.
S9. [theorem] The fundamental solution of u^2 - 7 v^2 = 1 is 8+3\sqrt{7}. For x mod 7 = 4, the positive solutions are generated by the seeds (x,y)=(4,1) and (11,4) using (x,y) -> (8x+21y, 3x+8y).
S10. [calc] First sequence from (4,1) -> <<(8*4+21*1,3*4+8*1)=(53,20)>>
S11. [calc] Continue the first sequence -> <<(8*53+21*20,3*53+8*20)=(844,319)>>
S12. [calc] Continue the first sequence -> <<(8*844+21*319,3*844+8*319)=(13451,5084)>>
S13. [calc] The next x in the first sequence exceeds the bound -> <<8*13451+21*5084=214372>>
S14. [calc] Second sequence from (11,4) -> <<(8*11+21*4,3*11+8*4)=(172,65)>>
S15. [calc] Continue the second sequence -> <<(8*172+21*65,3*172+8*65)=(2741,1036)>>
S16. [calc] The next x in the second sequence exceeds the bound -> <<8*2741+21*1036=43684>>
S17. [calc] Convert the largest admissible x from the first sequence to n -> <<(13451-4)/7=1921>>
S18. [calc] The largest admissible x from the second sequence gives a smaller n -> <<(2741-4)/7=391>>
S19. [derive] Since x=13451 is the largest admissible solution x<=14060 with x mod 7 = 4, the greatest possible n is 1921.

[Check]
V1. For n=1921, compute (n+1)(7n+1) -> <<1922*13448=25847056>>
V2. Verify that this value is a square -> <<5084*5084=25847056>>
V3. The transformed bound for n<=2008 is x<=14060, and x=7*1921+4=13451 is within this bound.
V4. The next solution x=214372 in the first sequence and the next solution x=43684 in the second sequence both exceed 14060, so no larger n up to 2008 works.

[Answer]
\boxed{1921}

solution:
[Overview]
This is a rational-root counting problem for a quartic with integer coefficients, fixed leading coefficient 9 and constant term 15, and arbitrary integer middle coefficients. The goal is to count distinct rational numbers that can occur as roots. The key idea is the Rational Root Theorem plus a check that every reduced candidate can be realized.

[Plan]
P1. Write a rational root as p/q in lowest terms.
P2. Use the Rational Root Theorem to restrict p and q.
P3. Enumerate reduced fractions for q = 1, 3, 9 and remove duplicates.
P4. Show every candidate can be made a root by choosing integer middle coefficients.
P5. Count the candidates and state the answer.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let r = p/q be a rational root with q > 0 and gcd(p,q) = 1. The polynomial equation gives 9(p/q)^4 + a_3(p/q)^3 + a_2(p/q)^2 + a_1(p/q) + 15 = 0.
S2. [theorem] By the Rational Root Theorem, p divides 15 and q divides 9. Thus p is in {1,-1,3,-3,5,-5,15,-15} and q is in {1,3,9}.
S3. [derive] For q = 1, all eight choices of p give distinct roots: 1, -1, 3, -3, 5, -5, 15, -15.
S4. [case] For q = 3, the condition gcd(p,3) = 1 leaves p in {1,-1,5,-5}. These give 1/3, -1/3, 5/3, -5/3.
S5. [case] For q = 9, the condition gcd(p,9) = 1 again leaves p in {1,-1,5,-5}. These give 1/9, -1/9, 5/9, -5/9.
S6. [calc] Add the counts from q = 1, 3, 9 -> <<8+4+4=16>>.
S7. [derive] Each counted fraction is realizable. For r = p/q, multiply the root equation by q^3/p to get a_1 q^2 + a_2 p q + a_3 p^2 = -9p^3/q - 15q^3/p. Since p divides 15 and q divides 9, the right side is an integer N. Also gcd(q^2, p q, p^2) = 1, so integers a_1, a_2, a_3 exist solving a_1 q^2 + a_2 p q + a_3 p^2 = N. Hence every listed fraction can occur as a rational root.

[Check]
V1. The unreduced raw list has 8*3 = 24 pairs, but reducing pairs such as 3/3 = 1 and 15/9 = 5/3 removes duplicates, leaving 16 distinct values.
V2. The construction in S7 covers every fraction with p dividing 15 and q dividing 9, so no candidate is merely formal; each is possible for some allowed integer coefficients.

[Answer]
\boxed{16}

S1. [setup] Let p, q, r be the roots of x^3 - 9x^2 + 8x + 2 = 0.
S2. [theorem] By Vieta's formulas, p+q+r=9, pq+pr+qr=8, and pqr=-2.

P1. Write the general coefficient in the expansion of (1 + ix)^2009.

S1. [setup] Expand {{(1+ix)^2009 = sum_{k=0}^{2009} C(2009,k) i^k x^k}} so the coefficient of x^k is C(2009,k) i^k.
S2. [derive] The coefficient C(2009,k) i^k is real exactly when i^k is real. This happens for even k, with value C(2009,k) when k = 0 mod 4 and value -C(2009,k) when k = 2 mod 4.
S3. [derive] Therefore the sum of all real coefficients is S = sum_{k=0}^{2009} C(2009,k) cos(k*pi/2).
S4. [derive] Evaluating the original expansion at x = 1 gives sum_{k=0}^{2009} C(2009,k) i^k = (1+i)^2009, so S = Re((1+i)^2009).
S5. [symbolic] Write 1+i in polar form -> {{1+i = sqrt(2)(cos(pi/4)+i sin(pi/4)) => (1+i)^2009 = (sqrt(2))^2009(cos(2009*pi/4)+i sin(2009*pi/4))}}

This is a constrained symmetric optimization problem. The goal is to maximize the smallest of the three pairwise products under fixed sum and fixed pairwise sum. The key idea is to order the variables, express the minimum as a product of the two smaller variables, reduce to two variables, and maximize a quadratic expression on its feasible interval.

[Plan]
P1. Order the variables so that the minimum pairwise product is identified.
P2. Introduce the sum and product of the two smaller variables.
P3. Use the two given constraints to express the product in terms of the sum.
P4. Determine the feasible interval from positivity, discriminant, and ordering conditions.
P5. Maximize the product on that interval and identify the equality case.
P6. Verify the candidate triple in the original constraints.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] By symmetry, reorder the positive numbers as a >= b >= c. Then m = min{ab,bc,ca} = bc. Let u=b+c and v=bc, so a=10-u.
S2. [derive] Using ab+ac+bc=25 gives a(b+c)+bc=(10-u)u+v=25. Hence v=25-10u+u^2=(u-5)^2.
S3. [derive] Since b and c are real, their discriminant must satisfy u^2-4v >= 0. Substituting v=(u-5)^2 gives -3u^2+40u-100 >= 0, that is, (3u-10)(10-u) >= 0. Because a>0 gives u<10, this implies u >= 10/3.
S4. [derive] The ordering condition a >= b means 10-u >= (u+sqrt(D))/2, where D=u^2-4v. This is equivalent to 20-3u >= sqrt(D). After squaring under u <= 20/3, it becomes (3u-25)(u-5) >= 0. Combining with u >= 10/3 and positivity v>0 gives 10/3 <= u < 5.
S5. [calc] Since v=(u-5)^2 decreases on this interval, its maximum is at u=10/3, giving v <= <<(10/3-5)^2=25/9>>.
S6. [derive] At u=10/3, the discriminant is zero, so b=c=u/2=5/3. Then a=10-u=20/3. Thus the equality case is (a,b,c)=(20/3,5/3,5/3), where bc=25/9 and the other two products are 100/9.

S1. [setup] Let d = x+z, p = x/d, and s = y/d. Then 0 < p < 1, s > 0, x=pd, z=(1-p)d, and y=sd.
S2. [derive] After substitution and cancellation of d, the expression becomes E = 4(1-p)/(2p+s) + 4p/(s+2-2p) + s.
S3. [setup] Set A=2p and B=2(1-p). Then A>0, B>0, A+B=2, and E = s + 2B/(s+A) + 2A/(s+B).

S2. [derive] The sum of the block is n(2b+n-1)/2. Setting this equal to 2014 gives n(2b+n-1)=4028.

P1. State that m is positive because the second conic is a hyperbola, and let a contact point be (x,y).

S5. [theorem] At a point of tangency, the two curves have equal tangent slopes.

P2. Combine those congruences using the least common multiple of 2 through 6.

S4. [derive] Since lcm(2,3,4,5,6) = 60, we have n = 1 mod 60, so n = 60m + 1 for some integer m.
S5. [derive] The number must also be divisible by 7, so 60m + 1 = 0 mod 7.
S6. [derive] Since 60 = 4 mod 7, this becomes 4m + 1 = 0 mod 7, so 4m = 6 mod 7.
S7. [symbolic] Multiply by the inverse of 4 modulo 7, which is 2 -> {{4m = 6 (mod 7) => m = 5 (mod 7)}}

[Plan]

P2. Factor 10 into possible factors greater than 1, corresponding to exponents plus one.

P4. Compare the resulting candidates and choose the smallest.

S2. [theorem] Use the divisor-count formula d(n) = (a1+1)(a2+1)... for the prime factorization of n.

S6. [case] For the factorization 5*2, the exponents are 4 and 1. To minimize, assign exponent 4 to prime 2 and exponent 1 to prime 3.

The goal is to maximize the number of distinct prime factors of a under the condition that a has fewer distinct prime factors than b. P1. Let x and y be the numbers of distinct prime factors of a and b.
P2. Translate the gcd and lcm conditions into intersection and union sizes.
