[Overview]
This is a trigonometric quadratic inequality problem. The goal is to find all angles theta for which a certain quadratic in x is strictly positive on the whole interval 0 <= x <= 1. The key idea is to use endpoint conditions and then impose positivity of the quadratic minimum.

[Plan]
P1. Write the expression as a quadratic in x with coefficients depending on sin theta and cos theta.
P2. Use the endpoint values at x = 0 and x = 1 to restrict theta.
P3. Locate the vertex of the quadratic and confirm it lies in the interval 0 <= x <= 1.
P4. Require the minimum value to be positive.
P5. Solve the resulting trigonometric inequality and verify endpoint behavior.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let c = cos theta and s = sin theta, and define Q(x) = c x^2 - x(1-x) + (1-x)^2 s.
S2. [derive] Evaluating at x = 0 gives Q(0) = s > 0, and at x = 1 gives Q(1) = c > 0. Hence theta must lie in the open first quadrant, so 0 < theta < pi/2.
S3. [symbolic] Expand Q(x) -> {{c x^2 - x(1-x) + (1-x)^2 s => (1+c+s)x^2 - (1+2s)x + s}}.
S4. [derive] Let A = 1+c+s and B = 1+2s, so Q(x) = A x^2 - B x + s. Since theta is in the first quadrant, A > 0, and the vertex x0 = B/(2A) satisfies 0 < x0 < 1.
S5. [symbolic] The minimum value on 0 <= x <= 1 is at x0 and equals s - B^2/(4A) -> {{s - (1+2s)^2/(4(1+c+s)) => (4cs-1)/(4(1+c+s))}}.
S6. [derive] Because the denominator 4(1+c+s) is positive, Q(x) > 0 for all 0 <= x <= 1 exactly when 4cs - 1 > 0.
S7. [derive] Since 4cs = 2 sin(2 theta), the condition becomes sin(2 theta) > 1/2. With 0 < theta < pi/2, this gives pi/6 < 2 theta < 5 pi/6, so pi/12 < theta < 5 pi/12.

[Check]
V1. At theta = pi/12, we have sin(2 theta) = 1/2, so the minimum value is 0, which violates the strict inequality.
V2. At theta = pi/4, we have 4 cos theta sin theta = 2 > 1, so the minimum is positive and the endpoints are positive, confirming the condition.

[Answer]
\boxed{(\pi/12,5\pi/12)}

[Plan]
P1. Let a_k = cos(2k*pi/7) for k=1,2,3.
P2. Rewrite 2 - sin^2(k*pi/7) in terms of a_k.
P3. Use the cubic equation satisfied by a_1,a_2,a_3.
P4. Compute the product of (a_k+3) and then the square root.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Define a_k = cos(2k*pi/7) for k=1,2,3. Then sin^2(k*pi/7) = (1-a_k)/2.
S2. [derive] The numbers a_1,a_2,a_3 are the roots of 8x^3+4x^2-4x-1=0, so the monic cubic is q(x)=x^3+(1/2)x^2-(1/2)x-1/8.
S3. [derive] Since q(x)=\prod_{k=1}^3 (x-a_k), we have \prod_{k=1}^3 (3+a_k) = -q(-3).
S4. [calc] Evaluate q(-3) -> <<(-3)^3+(1/2)(-3)^2-(1/2)(-3)-1/8=-169/8>>
S5. [derive] Therefore \prod_{k=1}^3 (3+a_k)=169/8.
S6. [derive] Also 2-sin^2(k*pi/7) = (3+a_k)/2, so the three-factor product is (1/8)*(169/8)=169/64.
S7. [calc] Take the positive square root -> <<sqrt(169/64)=13/8>>

V3. Since (13/8)^2 = 169/64 = 2.640625, the computed square root matches.

[Answer]

S1. [setup] Let A = arctan(1/3) + arctan(1/4) + arctan(1/5). The equation is A + arctan(1/n) = pi/4.

S4. [symbolic] Combine arctan(7/11) with arctan(1/5) -> {{(7/11 + 1/5)/(1 - (7/11)(1/5)) => 23/24}}
S5. [theorem] Since all intermediate sums lie in (0, pi/2), we have A = arctan(23/24).
S6. [symbolic] Use the tangent difference formula -> {{tan(pi/4 - A) => (1 - tan A)/(1 + tan A)}}

[Answer]

S1. [setup] Let the semicircle have radius 2, with A at angle 0 and B at angle pi. Put C_i at angle i*pi/7 for i = 1,2,...,6.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let P(z)=z^{20}-4z^{19}+9z^{18}-16z^{17}+\cdots+441, let z_1,\ldots,z_{20} be its roots, let alpha_k=\operatorname{arccot} z_k, and let T=\sum_{k=1}^{20}\alpha_k. Branch changes add integer multiples of pi and do not affect \cot T.
S2. [derive] Since \cot alpha_k=z_k, we have e^{2i\alpha_k}=(z_k+i)/(z_k-i), so e^{2iT}=\prod_{k=1}^{20}(z_k+i)/(z_k-i).

[Overview]
This is a trigonometric sequence problem. The goal is to find the least positive real value of t for which four arcsin-sine values can form a geometric progression for some \alpha in (0,\pi/2). The key idea is to use the first three terms to determine the possible common ratios, then choose the smallest t that realizes the fourth term.

[Plan]
P1. Define the four terms and use the geometric progression condition on the first three terms.
P2. Split the interval for \alpha according to the formula for \arcsin(\sin 2\alpha).
P3. Solve the resulting equations for possible \alpha.
P4. Compute the common ratio r for each valid \alpha and determine the least t from the fourth term.
P5. Compare the candidates and verify the least value.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let a_k=\arcsin(\sin(k\alpha)) for k=1,2,7,t. Since 0<\alpha<\pi/2, we have a_1=\alpha. If a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4 is a GP with ratio r, then r=a_2/a_1>0 and a_4=a_1r^3.

S2. [case] If 0<\alpha<\pi/4, then a_2=2\alpha, so r=2. The condition a_3=a_1r^2 becomes \arcsin(\sin 7\alpha)=4\alpha. Since the right side is at most \pi/2, \alpha\le\pi/8. In this range the equation gives \alpha=\pi/11. Then a_4=a_1r^3=8\pi/11>\pi/2, impossible because every arcsin value is at most \pi/2. So this case gives no four-term GP.

S3. [case] If \alpha=\pi/4, then a_2=\pi/2 and r=2, so a_3 would equal \pi, impossible. Thus \alpha\ne\pi/4.

S4. [case] If \pi/4<\alpha<\pi/2, then a_2=\pi-2\alpha. Write x=\alpha/\pi, so 1/4<x<1/2. The GP condition is
a_3=\frac{a_2^2}{a_1}=\pi\frac{(1-2x)^2}{x}.
Let h(x)=\frac{(1-2x)^2}{x}. Since a_3\le\pi/2, we need h(x)\le1/2.

S5. [derive] In the allowed range, the equation a_3=\arcsin(\sin 7\alpha) becomes \pi h(x)=\arcsin(\sin 7\pi x). The possible congruences are 7x=2+h(x) and 7x=3-h(x). Solving h(x)=7x-2 gives x=1/3. Solving h(x)=3-7x gives 11x^2-7x+1=0, so x=(7+\sqrt5)/22 or x=(7-\sqrt5)/22; only x=(7+\sqrt5)/22 lies in the allowed interval.

S6. [symbolic] For x=(7+\sqrt5)/22, compute the common ratio -> {{r = (1-2x)/x => (3-\sqrt5)/2}}

S7. [symbolic] The least t for this \alpha is r^3, so cube the ratio -> {{((3-\sqrt5)/2)^3 => 9-4\sqrt5}}

S8. [derive] For any valid GP, the fourth term is a_1r^3. Since 0<a_4\le\pi/2, the smallest positive t satisfying \arcsin(\sin(t\alpha))=a_4 is t=a_4/\alpha=r^3. The possible ratios are r=2 for \alpha=\pi/11, which gives no fourth term; r=1 for \alpha=\pi/3, giving t=1; and r=(3-\sqrt5)/2, giving t=9-4\sqrt5. Since 9-4\sqrt5<1, the least value is attained at \alpha=\pi(7+\sqrt5)/22.

[Check]
V1. For \alpha=\pi(7+\sqrt5)/22 and t=9-4\sqrt5, the first three terms have common ratio r=(3-\sqrt5)/2 by construction.
V2. The fourth term equals a_1r^3=t\alpha, and since 0<t\alpha<\pi/2, \arcsin(\sin(t\alpha))=t\alpha. Thus the four terms form a GP.
V3. The numerical value is t=9-4\sqrt5\approx0.055728, which is smaller than the other realizable candidate t=1.

[Answer]
\boxed{9-4\sqrt{5}}

[Overview]
This is a trigonometric identifiability problem. The goal is to find all possible values on Malvina's card that allow her, after all three values are shared, to uniquely determine the function while the other two students cannot. The key idea is to analyze when the multiset {sin x, cos x, tan x} determines the function assignment uniquely and when a repeated value creates ambiguity.

[Plan]
P1. Set s = sin x, c = cos x, and t = tan x, so the students know the multiset {s,c,t}.
P2. Determine when the multiset allows more than one function assignment for a given value.
P3. Analyze the cases where exactly one student can identify her function.
P4. Collect all possible identifiable values on Malvina's card and sum them.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let s = sin x, c = cos x, and t = tan x = s/c, where 0 < x < 90 degrees. After sharing, every student knows the multiset {s,c,t} and her own value.
S2. [derive] If s,c,t are pairwise distinct, checking the possible reassignments of which value is tan y for another acute angle y shows that the only new multiset would require t = c, giving a repeated value. Thus, with distinct values, the multiset determines x and the function assignment, so all three students could identify their functions.
S3. [case] Repeated values occur only when s = c, or when t = c. The equality s = t would imply c = 1, impossible for acute x.
S4. [derive] If s = c, then x = 45 degrees, with s = c = sqrt(2)/2 and t = 1. The multiset is {sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(2)/2, 1}. The holder of 1 can identify it as tan, while the two holders of sqrt(2)/2 cannot distinguish sin from cos.
S5. [derive] If t = c, then s/c = c, so s = c^2. Since s^2 + c^2 = 1, we get s^2 + s - 1 = 0, hence s = (sqrt(5) - 1)/2. The multiset is {s,c,c}. The holder of s can identify it as sin, while the two holders of c cannot distinguish cos from tan.
S6. [case] In both repeated-value cases, exactly one value has a unique function assignment: 1 in the first case and (sqrt(5) - 1)/2 in the second case.
S7. [derive] Therefore, the only possible values on Malvina's card are 1 and (sqrt(5) - 1)/2.
S8. [calc] Sum the possible values -> <<1+(sqrt(5)-1)/2=(sqrt(5)+1)/2>>.

[Check]
V1. For x = 45 degrees, the multiset {sqrt(2)/2, sqrt(2)/2, 1} lets only the holder of 1 identify the function, namely tan.
V2. For the other case, s = (sqrt(5) - 1)/2 satisfies s^2 + s - 1 = 0, giving t = c and multiset {s,c,c}; only s is uniquely identifiable, as sin.
V3. The sum 1 + (sqrt(5) - 1)/2 equals (sqrt(5) + 1)/2, consistent with the calculation.

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{\sqrt5+1}{2}}

[Overview]
This is a triangle area-ratio problem. The goal is to compute [PQR]/[ABC] for the small triangle formed by three cevians. The key idea is to use affine invariance to place the triangle at convenient coordinates, find the three intersection points, and compute the area ratio.

[Plan]
P1. Choose convenient coordinates for triangle ABC using affine invariance.
P2. Determine the coordinates of D, E, and F from the given ratios.
P3. Find equations for lines AD, BE, and CF.
P4. Compute the intersections P, Q, and R.
P5. Calculate the area of triangle PQR and divide by the area of ABC.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] By affine invariance, set A=(0,0), B=(1,0), and C=(0,1). Then [ABC]=1/2.
S2. [derive] From BD:DC=1:2, D=(2/3,1/3); from CE:EA=1:2, E=(0,2/3); from AF:FB=1:2, F=(1/3,0).
S3. [derive] The cevians have equations AD: y=x/2, BE: 2x+3y=2, and CF: 3x+y=1.
S4. [derive] Solving the line intersections gives P=(2/7,1/7), Q=(4/7,2/7), and R=(1/7,4/7).
S5. [calc] Twice the area of PQR is the absolute determinant of Q-P and R-P -> <<abs((4/7-2/7)*(4/7-1/7)-(2/7-1/7)*(1/7-2/7))=1/7>>
S6. [derive] Since twice the area of PQR is 1/7, [PQR]=1/14.
S7. [calc] Compute the desired ratio -> <<(1/14)/(1/2)=1/7>>

[Check]
V1. Routh theorem with ratios x=y=z=1/2 gives ((xyz-1)^2)/((xy+x+1)(yz+y+1)(zx+z+1))=1/7, agreeing.
V2. The value 1/7 lies between 0 and 1, as required for an area ratio.

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{1}{7}}

[Overview]
This is a trigonometric optimization problem. The goal is to find the minimum value of a rational expression in sin x and cos x. The key idea is to set s = sin^2 x and c = cos^2 x, reducing the expression to a one-variable function of p = sc.

[Plan]
P1. Introduce s = sin^2 x and c = cos^2 x with s + c = 1.
P2. Express sin^6 x + cos^6 x and sin^4 x + cos^4 x in terms of p = sc.
P3. Write the given quotient as a function of p.
P4. Determine the allowed interval for p using s + c = 1.
P5. Use monotonicity to locate the minimum and verify it.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let s = sin^2 x and c = cos^2 x. Then s >= 0, c >= 0, and s + c = 1.
S2. [setup] Let p = sc = sin^2 x cos^2 x.
S3. [symbolic] Compute the sixth-power sum -> {{sin^6 x + cos^6 x = s^3 + c^3 = (s+c)^3 - 3sc(s+c) => 1 - 3p}}
S4. [symbolic] Compute the fourth-power sum -> {{sin^4 x + cos^4 x = s^2 + c^2 = (s+c)^2 - 2sc => 1 - 2p}}
S5. [symbolic] Rewrite the quotient -> {{(sin^6 x + cos^6 x + 1)/(sin^4 x + cos^4 x + 1) = ((1-3p)+1)/((1-2p)+1) => (2-3p)/(2-2p)}}
S6. [derive] Since s + c = 1 and s,c >= 0, the product satisfies 0 <= p = sc <= (s+c)^2/4 = 1/4.
S7. [derive] Let f(p) = (2-3p)/(2-2p). Then f'(p) = -2/(2-2p)^2 < 0, so f is decreasing on [0,1/4].
S8. [calc] The minimum occurs at p = 1/4 and equals <<(2-3*(1/4))/(2-2*(1/4))=5/6>>.
S9. [case] Equality p = 1/4 requires s = c = 1/2, which is attainable when sin^2 x = cos^2 x = 1/2.

[Check]
V1. Substitute p = 1/4 into the reduced function -> <<(2-3/4)/(2-1/2)=5/6>>.
V2. Check the other endpoint p = 0 -> <<(2-0)/(2-0)=1>>, which is greater than 5/6.
V3. Directly at x = pi/4, the numerator is 1/8 + 1/8 + 1 = 5/4 and the denominator is 1/4 + 1/4 + 1 = 3/2, giving (5/4)/(3/2) = 5/6.

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{5}{6}}

solution:
[Overview]
This is a vector geometry problem involving the altitudes of an acute triangle. The goal is to determine angle ACB from a linear relation among the three altitude vectors. The key idea is to place the triangle in coordinates, express each altitude vector in terms of the side ratio and the cosine and sine of angle C, and solve the resulting component equations.

[Plan]
P1. Set coordinates with C at the origin and A on the positive x-axis.
P2. Express B using the side length ratio r = BC/AC and the angle at C.
P3. Compute the three altitude vectors AD, BE, and CF in coordinates.
P4. Use both components of the given vector equation to form equations in r and cos C.
P5. Solve for cos C and then determine angle C.
P6. Check the result by substitution into the original vector equation.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Scale so AC = 1 and place C=(0,0), A=(1,0). Let u=\cos C and v=\sin C, where C = angle ACB. Let BC=r, so B=(r u,r v), with v>0.

S2. [derive] The foot D of A onto line BC is D=(u^2,u v), so
\vec{AD}=(-v^2,u v).
The foot E of B onto CA is E=(r u,0), so
\vec{BE}=(0,-r v).

S3. [derive] Let L^2=AB^2=1+r^2-2r u. Projecting C onto line AB gives the foot F and hence
\vec{CF}=\left(\frac{r^2 v^2}{L^2},\frac{r(1-r u)v}{L^2}\right).

S4. [derive] Substitute into
9\vec{AD}+4\vec{BE}+7\vec{CF}=0.
The x-component gives
-9v^2+\frac{7r^2v^2}{L^2}=0.
The y-component, after dividing by v, gives
9u-4r+\frac{7r(1-r u)}{L^2}=0.

S5. [derive] Since v>0, the x-component yields L^2=\frac{7r^2}{9}. Substituting this into the y-component gives
9u-4r+\frac{9}{r}(1-r u)=0.
The terms 9u and -9u cancel, leaving
-4r+\frac{9}{r}=0.

S6. [derive] Thus 4r^2=9. Because r>0, r=\frac{3}{2}. Then
L^2=\frac{7r^2}{9}=\frac{7}{4}.
Using L^2=1+r^2-2r u gives
\frac{7}{4}=1+\frac{9}{4}-3u,
so u=\frac{1}{2}.

S7. [derive] Since u=\cos C=\frac{1}{2} and C is acute, we have C=60^\circ.

[Check]
V1. For C=60^\circ and r=3/2, we have u=1/2, v=\sqrt{3}/2, and L^2=7/4.
V2. The altitude vectors are \vec{AD}=(-3/4,\sqrt{3}/4), \vec{BE}=(0,-3\sqrt{3}/4), and \vec{CF}=(27/28,3\sqrt{3}/28).
V3. Substitution gives 9\vec{AD}+4\vec{BE}+7\vec{CF}=(0,0), so the original vector equation is satisfied.
V4. The triangle is acute for these values because r u=3/4<1 and u<r, so the altitude feet lie on the corresponding sides.

[Answer]
\boxed{60^\circ}

[Overview]
This is a trigonometric simplification using 13th roots of unity. The goal is to evaluate the sum of three cosines. The key idea is to identify the angles with quadratic residues modulo 13 and use the quadratic Gauss period.

[Plan]
P1. Define the 13th roots of unity and the set of quadratic residues modulo 13.
P2. Pair each residue term with its negative to relate the root-of-unity sum to the given cosine sum.
P3. Use the quadratic Gauss sum for the prime 13 to evaluate the relevant period.
P4. Solve for the required cosine sum and verify the result numerically.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let z = e^{2\pi i/13}. The quadratic residues modulo 13 are QR = {1,3,4,9,10,12}. Define S = \sum_{a \in QR} z^a.
S2. [derive] Since -1 is a quadratic residue modulo 13, the set QR is closed under negation. Therefore the terms pair as z^1 with z^12, z^3 with z^10, and z^4 with z^9, giving S = 2(\cos(2\pi/13) + \cos(6\pi/13) + \cos(8\pi/13)).
S3. [theorem] For an odd prime p, the quadratic Gauss sum satisfies G = \sum_{a=1}^{p-1} (a/p) z^a, and for p = 13, since 13 \equiv 1 \pmod 4, one has G = \sqrt{13}.
S4. [derive] Let T be the sum of z^a over nonresidue exponents modulo 13. Then G = S - T, while S + T = \sum_{a=1}^{12} z^a = -1.
S5. [symbolic] Solve the two equations for S -> {{S - T = \sqrt{13}, S + T = -1 => S = (\sqrt{13}-1)/2}}.
S6. [symbolic] Use S = 2E, where E is the required cosine sum, to solve for E -> {{S = 2E and S = (\sqrt{13}-1)/2 => E = (\sqrt{13}-1)/4}}.

[Check]
V1. Numerically, the original sum is about 0.6514, and (\sqrt{13}-1)/4 is about 0.6514, so the value is consistent.
V2. Multiplying the answer by 2 gives (\sqrt{13}-1)/2, which matches the computed real Gaussian period S.

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{\sqrt{13}-1}{4}}

S3. [derive] Applying R once sends x_parallel + x_perp to x_parallel - x_perp.
S4. [derive] Applying R again sends x_parallel - x_perp to x_parallel - (-x_perp) = x_parallel + x_perp = x.

[Answer]

[Overview]
This is a trigonometric geometry problem. The goal is to find all possible values of x for which an isosceles triangle has equal sides cos x, base cos 7x, and vertex angle 2x. The key idea is to use the law of cosines to get cos 7x = sin 2x, then solve the resulting cosine equation with triangle restrictions.

[Plan]
P1. Set up the equal sides, base, and vertex angle of the isosceles triangle.
P2. Use the law of cosines to relate the base to the equal sides and vertex angle.
P3. Simplify the relation to a trigonometric equation.
P4. Solve the trigonometric equation using general cosine equality.
P5. Restrict the solutions to the valid triangle angle range and verify them.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let the equal sides be a = cos x, the base be b = cos 7x, and the vertex angle between the equal sides be 2x. Since the triangle is nondegenerate, 0 < 2x < 180, so 0 < x < 90.

S2. [theorem] By the law of cosines applied to the two equal sides, b^2 = a^2 + a^2 - 2a^2 cos(2x).

S3. [derive] Since 1 - cos(2x) = 2 sin^2 x, we get b^2 = 4a^2 sin^2 x. Because a > 0 and sin x > 0 on 0 < x < 90, this gives b = 2a sin x.

S4. [derive] Substitute a = cos x and b = cos 7x to obtain cos 7x = 2 cos x sin x = sin 2x. Since sin 2x = cos(90 - 2x), the equation is cos 7x = cos(90 - 2x).

S5. [theorem] For real angles A and B, cos A = cos B exactly when A = B + 360k or A = -B + 360k for some integer k.

S6. [case] Using A = 7x and B = 90 - 2x, the first case is 7x = 90 - 2x + 360k. This gives 9x = 90 + 360k, so x = 10 + 40k. With 0 < x < 90, the valid values are k = 0 and k = 1, giving x = 10 and x = 50.

S7. [case] The second case is 7x = -(90 - 2x) + 360k, so 7x = -90 + 2x + 360k. This gives 5x = -90 + 360k, so x = -18 + 72k. With 0 < x < 90, the only valid value is k = 1, giving x = 54.

S8. [derive] The candidate values are therefore 10, 50, and 54. For each, 0 < x < 90 gives positive equal sides cos x, and cos 7x = sin 2x = 2 cos x sin x > 0. Also 2 cos x sin x < 2 cos x because sin x < 1, so the triangle inequality holds.

[Check]
V1. For x = 10, cos 70 = sin 20 = 2 cos 10 sin 10, so the side and angle relation holds.
V2. For x = 50, cos 350 = cos 10 = sin 80 = sin 100 = 2 cos 50 sin 50, so the relation holds.
V3. For x = 54, cos 378 = cos 18 = sin 72 = sin 108 = 2 cos 54 sin 54, so the relation holds.
V4. All three values satisfy 0 < x < 90 and produce positive side lengths with vertex angles 20, 100, and 108 degrees respectively, so all are valid.

[Answer]
\boxed{10, 50, 54}

[Overview]
This is a trigonometric counting problem. The goal is to compute the sum of F(n) for n from 2 to 2007, where F(n) counts solutions of sin x = sin nx on [0, pi]. The key idea is to use the general sine equality condition, count two families of solutions, subtract overlaps, and then sum the resulting formula.

[Plan]
P1. Translate sin x = sin nx into two congruence families.
P2. Count the solutions from the first family on [0, pi].
P3. Count the solutions from the second family on [0, pi].
P4. Determine when the two families overlap and subtract those duplicated points.
P5. Write a closed formula for F(n).
P6. Sum the formula from n = 2 to 2007 and subtract the overlap correction totals.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] For each n > 1, count the distinct x in [0, pi] satisfying sin x = sin nx.
S2. [derive] Since sin A = sin B exactly when A = B + 2k pi or A = pi - B + 2k pi, the solutions split into x = nx + 2k pi and x = pi - nx + 2k pi for integers k.
S3. [derive] The first family gives x = 2m pi/(n-1) with integer m. The condition 0 <= x <= pi gives 0 <= m <= (n-1)/2, so this family has floor((n-1)/2)+1 = ceil(n/2) solutions.
S4. [derive] The second family gives x = (2k+1) pi/(n+1) with integer k. The condition 0 <= x <= pi gives positive odd integers 2k+1 <= n+1, so this family has floor(n/2)+1 solutions.
S5. [derive] A point can belong to both families only when 2x = pi mod 2pi, so in [0, pi] the only possible common point is x = pi/2. This point is a solution exactly when sin(n pi/2) = 1, which happens exactly when n mod 4 = 1.
S6. [derive] Thus F(n) = ceil(n/2) + floor(n/2) + 1 - d(n), where d(n) = 1 if n mod 4 = 1 and d(n) = 0 otherwise. Since ceil(n/2)+floor(n/2)=n, we get F(n) = n+1-d(n).
S7. [calc] Sum n from 2 to 2007 -> <<(2+2007)*2006/2=2015027>>
S8. [calc] Add the constant 1 over the 2006 terms -> <<2015027+2006=2017033>>
S9. [derive] The integers n in [2, 2007] with n mod 4 = 1 are 5, 9, ..., 2005, and their count is (2005-5)/4+1.
S10. [calc] Count those correction terms -> <<(2005-5)/4+1=501>>
S11. [calc] Subtract the correction from the sum -> <<2017033-501=2016532>>

[Check]
V1. For n = 2, the formula gives F(2) = 3, which matches sin x = sin 2x giving x = 0, pi/3, pi.
V2. For n = 5, the formula gives F(5) = 5 after subtracting the common point x = pi/2, matching a direct family count.
V3. The final sum uses 2006 terms, includes the constant +2006, and subtracts exactly 501 values of n with n mod 4 = 1, so the arithmetic is consistent.

[Answer]
\boxed{2016532}

[Plan]
P1. State the dot product condition for perpendicular direction vectors.
P2. Form the dot product equation using the given vectors.
P3. Solve the resulting linear equation for a.
P4. Verify the solution by substitution.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let v1 = (3, -7) and v2 = (a, 2) be the two direction vectors.
S2. [theorem] Two nonzero vectors are perpendicular exactly when their dot product is zero.
S3. [derive] Apply the dot product condition: 3*a + (-7)*2 = 0.
S4. [symbolic] Solve the equation -> {{3a - 14 = 0 => a = 14/3}}

[Check]
V1. Substitute a = 14/3 into the dot product -> <<3*(14/3) + (-7)*2 = 0>>
V2. The dot product is zero, so the direction vectors are perpendicular.

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{14}{3}}

[Overview]
This is a line-plane intersection problem. The goal is to find where the line through the two given points meets the xy-plane. The key idea is to use a parametric equation of the line and set z = 0.

[Plan]
P1. Write a parametric equation for the line through the two given points.
P2. Use the condition z = 0 for the xy-plane.
P3. Solve for the parameter value.
P4. Substitute that parameter value into the x- and y-coordinates.
P5. State the intersection point.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let A = (3,4,1) and B = (5,1,6). A direction vector is B - A = (2,-3,5), so the line is P(t) = (3,4,1) + t(2,-3,5) = (3+2t, 4-3t, 1+5t).
S2. [derive] The xy-plane is z = 0, so require 1 + 5t = 0.
S3. [symbolic] Solve for t -> {{1 + 5t = 0 => t = -1/5}}
S4. [calc] Compute the x-coordinate -> <<3 + 2*(-1/5) = 13/5>>
S5. [calc] Compute the y-coordinate -> <<4 - 3*(-1/5) = 23/5>>
S6. [setup] Since z = 0 at this parameter value, the intersection point is (13/5, 23/5, 0).

[Check]
V1. Substitute t = -1/5 into the z-coordinate -> <<1 + 5*(-1/5) = 0>>, so the point lies in the xy-plane.
V2. The displacement from A to the point is (13/5-3, 23/5-4, 0-1) = (-2/5, 3/5, -1), which is (-1/5)(2,-3,5), so the point lies on the given line.

[Answer]
\boxed{\left(\frac{13}{5},\frac{23}{5},0\right)}

[Overview]
This is a matrix powers problem involving a rotation matrix. The goal is to find the smallest positive exponent n for which the matrix power is the identity matrix. The key idea is that the matrix represents a rotation by 170 degrees, so its nth power rotates by 170n degrees.

[Plan]
P1. Identify the given matrix as a rotation matrix.
P2. Use the rule for composing rotations to express the nth power.
P3. Translate the identity condition into an angle-multiple condition.
P4. Solve for the smallest positive integer n satisfying the divisibility condition.
P5. Verify the exponent in the original matrix power.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let A be the given matrix. Then A is the rotation matrix through 170 degrees, so A = R_{170}.
S2. [theorem] For rotations, R_a R_b = R_{a+b}; therefore A^n = R_{170n}.
S3. [theorem] A rotation R_theta equals the identity matrix exactly when theta is a multiple of 360 degrees.
S4. [derive] Thus A^n = I exactly when 170n is divisible by 360, which requires 360 divides 170n.
S5. [calc] The smallest such n is 360 divided by gcd(170,360) -> <<gcd(170,360)=10>>.
S6. [calc] Therefore the smallest positive n is -> <<360/10=36>>.

[Check]
V1. Substitute n = 36: 170*36 = 6120 = 17*360, so A^36 = R_{6120} = R_0 = I.
V2. The divisibility condition 360 | 170n reduces to 36 | n, so no smaller positive n works.

[Answer]
\boxed{36}

[Overview]
This is a vector identity problem involving the vector triple product, unit vectors, and linear independence. The goal is to find the angle between a and b. The key idea is to use the vector triple product identity and compare coefficients of the linearly independent vectors b and c.

[Plan]
P1. Apply the vector triple product identity to expand the left side.
P2. Express both sides as linear combinations of b and c.
P3. Use linear independence to set the coefficients of b and c to zero.
P4. Obtain the dot product a.b and convert it to the angle between a and b.
P5. Verify the result using the unit vector condition.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let theta be the angle between \mathbf a and \mathbf b, and set x=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b and y=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c.
S2. [theorem] Use the vector triple product identity \mathbf a\times(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)=\mathbf b(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf c)-\mathbf c(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b).
S3. [symbolic] Substitute x and y into the given equation -> {{ \mathbf b y-\mathbf c x=(1/\sqrt{2})\mathbf b+(1/\sqrt{2})\mathbf c => (y-1/\sqrt{2})\mathbf b+(-x-1/\sqrt{2})\mathbf c=0 }}
S4. [derive] Since \{\mathbf a,\mathbf b,\mathbf c\} is linearly independent, the vectors \mathbf b and \mathbf c are linearly independent, so both coefficients in the relation above must be zero.
S5. [symbolic] Solve the coefficient equations -> {{ y-1/\sqrt{2}=0, -x-1/\sqrt{2}=0 => y=1/\sqrt{2}, x=-1/\sqrt{2} }}
S6. [derive] Because \mathbf a and \mathbf b are unit vectors, x=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=\cos\theta, so \cos\theta=-1/\sqrt{2}.
S7. [calc] Find the angle in degrees -> <<180/pi*acos(-1/sqrt(2))=135>>

[Check]
V1. The value \cos 135^\circ=-1/\sqrt{2} matches x=\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b.
V2. Substituting y=1/\sqrt{2} and x=-1/\sqrt{2} gives \mathbf b y-\mathbf c x=(1/\sqrt{2})\mathbf b+(1/\sqrt{2})\mathbf c, which is the required right side.
V3. The vector \mathbf a is not forced to lie in the span of \mathbf b and \mathbf c, so linear independence remains possible.

[Answer]
\boxed{135^\circ}

[Overview]
This is a matrix-vector equation problem. The goal is to find the vector v satisfying a polynomial in A applied to v equals (0, 11)^T. The key idea is that A^2 = 3I, so every even power of A is a scalar multiple of I.

[Plan]
P1. Compute A^2.
P2. Use A^2 = 3I to express A^4, A^6, and A^8 as scalar multiples of I.
P3. Sum the coefficients of I in the given matrix polynomial.
P4. Solve the resulting scalar multiple of I times v.
P5. Verify the answer by substitution.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let v = (x, y)^T and set A = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 3 & 0\end{pmatrix}.
S2. [symbolic] Compute A squared -> {{A^2 = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 3 & 0\end{pmatrix}^2 => \begin{pmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{pmatrix} = 3I}}
S3. [symbolic] Use A^2 = 3I to compute higher even powers -> {{A^4 = 9I,\ A^6 = 27I,\ A^8 = 81I}}
S4. [symbolic] Sum the scalar coefficients of I -> {{A^8 + A^6 + A^4 + A^2 + I = (81 + 27 + 9 + 3 + 1)I => 121I}}
S5. [derive] The equation becomes 121I v = \begin{pmatrix}0 \\ 11\end{pmatrix}, so 121v = \begin{pmatrix}0 \\ 11\end{pmatrix}.
S6. [symbolic] Solve for v -> {{v = \frac{1}{121}\begin{pmatrix}0 \\ 11\end{pmatrix} => \begin{pmatrix}0 \\ 11/121\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0 \\ 1/11\end{pmatrix}}}

[Check]
V1. Since the matrix polynomial simplifies to 121I, its product with v is 121v.
V2. Substitute v = (0, 1/11)^T -> <<121*(0,1/11)=(0,11)>>.

[Answer]
\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}0 \\ \frac{1}{11}\end{pmatrix}}

solution:
[Overview]
This is a trigonometric identity problem. The goal is to express sqrt(9 - 8 sin 50 degrees) as a + b csc 50 degrees with integers a and b. The key idea is to set x = sin 50 degrees and use the triple-angle identity to show that 3 - csc 50 degrees is the positive square root.

[Plan]
P1. Set x = sin 50 degrees and write csc 50 degrees as 1/x.
P2. Use sin 150 degrees and the triple-angle formula to obtain a polynomial relation for x.
P3. Show that (3 - 1/x)^2 equals 9 - 8x using that relation.
P4. Verify the positive square root sign and identify a and b.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let x = sin 50 degrees. Then csc 50 degrees = 1/x, and x > 0.
S2. [theorem] Use the triple-angle identity sin(3 theta) = 3 sin theta - 4 sin^3 theta with theta = 50 degrees.
S3. [symbolic] Since sin 150 degrees = 1/2, substitute x -> {{3*x - 4*x^3 = 1/2 => 8*x^3 - 6*x + 1 = 0}}.
S4. [symbolic] Divide the relation by x^2 -> {{(8*x^3 - 6*x + 1)/x^2 = 0 => 1/x^2 = 6/x - 8*x}}.
S5. [symbolic] Expand and substitute this relation -> {{(3 - 1/x)^2 = 9 - 6/x + 1/x^2 = 9 - 6/x + (6/x - 8*x) => 9 - 8*x}}.
S6. [derive] Thus (3 - 1/x)^2 = 9 - 8x, so sqrt(9 - 8x) = |3 - 1/x|.
S7. [derive] Since sin 50 degrees > sin 30 degrees = 1/2, we have 1/x < 2, so 3 - 1/x > 0.
S8. [derive] Therefore sqrt(9 - 8x) = 3 - 1/x.
S9. [derive] Replacing x by sin 50 degrees gives sqrt(9 - 8 sin 50 degrees) = 3 - csc 50 degrees = 3 + (-1)csc 50 degrees.
S10. [derive] Comparing with a + b csc 50 degrees gives a = 3 and b = -1.

[Check]
V1. The step 8*x^3 - 6*x + 1 = 0 follows from sin 150 degrees = 1/2 using the triple-angle identity.
V2. Squaring 3 - csc 50 degrees gives 9 - 8 sin 50 degrees, so the equality is exact.
V3. Since sin 50 degrees > 1/2, we have csc 50 degrees < 2, hence 3 - csc 50 degrees is positive and equals the positive square root.
V4. Therefore the ordered pair is (a,b) = (3,-1).

[Answer]
\boxed{(3,-1)}

S5. [derive] Using normal vector (2,0,1) and point (1,2,3), the plane is 2(x-1) + 0(y-2) + 1(z-3) = 0.
S6. [symbolic] Simplify the equation -> {{2(x-1) + 0(y-2) + 1(z-3) = 0 => 2x+z-5=0}}

[Overview]
This is a coordinate geometry and trigonometry problem. The goal is to find sin(2 angle BPC). The key idea is to place the equally spaced points on the x-axis, express the tangent of an angle subtended by two collinear points from P, and use the two given cosines to determine the geometry.

[Plan]
P1. Place the four points at equally spaced integer coordinates and let P be a general point above the line.
P2. Use the given cosine values to find the tangents of angle APC and angle BPD.
P3. Write the tangent equations for those two angles in terms of the coordinates of P.
P4. Eliminate one coordinate and solve for the vertical coordinate.
P5. Compute the tangent of angle BPC and then compute sin(2 angle BPC).
P6. Verify the solution against the original equations.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Set B=(0,0), A=(-1,0), C=(1,0), D=(2,0), and P=(x,y) with y>0; reflection handles y<0. For endpoints (u,0) and (v,0) with v>u, the signed tangent of the angle they subtend at P is tan = y(v-u)/(y^2+(u-x)(v-x)).
S2. [calc] Since cos(angle APC)=4/5 and the angle is acute, tan(angle APC)=sqrt(1-(4/5)^2)/(4/5) -> <<(sqrt(1-(4/5)^2))/(4/5)=3/4>>.
S3. [calc] Since cos(angle BPD)=3/5 and the angle is acute, tan(angle BPD)=sqrt(1-(3/5)^2)/(3/5) -> <<(sqrt(1-(3/5)^2))/(3/5)=4/3>>.
S4. [derive] Applying the tangent formula to A=(-1,0) and C=(1,0) gives 2y/(y^2+x^2-1)=3/4, which is equivalent to 3(x^2+y^2)-8y-3=0.
S5. [derive] Applying the tangent formula to B=(0,0) and D=(2,0) gives 2y/(y^2+x^2-2x)=4/3, which is equivalent to 2(x^2+y^2)-4x-3y=0.
S6. [derive] Let U=x^2+y^2. The two equations give U=(8y+3)/3 and 2U=4x+3y, so x=(7y+6)/12.
S7. [symbolic] Substitute x=(7y+6)/12 into x^2+y^2=(8y+3)/3 -> {{x=(7y+6)/12, x^2+y^2=(8y+3)/3 => 193y^2-300y-108=0}}.
S8. [calc] Because y>0, solve the quadratic for y -> <<(300+sqrt(300^2+4*193*108))/(2*193)=(150+12*sqrt(301))/193>>.
S9. [symbolic] For theta=angle BPC, tan(theta)=y/(y^2+x^2-x). Using U=(8y+3)/3 and x=(7y+6)/12 gives tan(theta)=12y/(25y+6), so t=tan(theta) satisfies -> {{t=12y/(25y+6), 193y^2-300y-108=0 => 9t^2-25t+9=0}}.
S10. [symbolic] From 9t^2-25t+9=0, 9(1+t^2)=25t, hence sin(2theta)=2t/(1+t^2) -> {{2t/(1+t^2) => 18/25}}.

[Check]
V1. The two coordinate equations in S4 and S5 are exactly the tangent forms of the given cosines, and the positive root for y ensures the denominators are positive as required by the acute angles.
V2. The value 18/25 is between 0 and 1, and substituting it back through t gives 9t^2-25t+9=0, consistent with the derived quadratic relation.

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{18}{25}}

[Overview]
This is a trigonometric exact-value problem. The goal is to compute cos 72 degrees. The key idea is to use the angle 36 degrees and the identities for cos(2x) and cos(3x), together with 5*36 = 180.

[Plan]
P1. Let y = cos 36 degrees and relate cos 72 degrees to cos 108 degrees using 3*36 + 2*36 = 180.
P2. Apply double-angle and triple-angle identities to form an equation in y.
P3. Factor the resulting cubic equation.
P4. Choose the positive root for cos 36 degrees.
P5. Use the double-angle identity to compute cos 72 degrees.
P6. Verify the result by substitution and a numerical sanity check.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let y = cos 36 degrees. Since 3*36 + 2*36 = 180, we have cos(3*36) = -cos(2*36).
S2. [theorem] Use cos(2x) = 2cos^2 x - 1 and cos(3x) = 4cos^3 x - 3cos x.
S3. [derive] Substituting x = 36 and y = cos 36 gives 4y^3 - 3y = -(2y^2 - 1), so 4y^3 + 2y^2 - 3y - 1 = 0.
S4. [symbolic] Factor the polynomial -> {{4y^3 + 2y^2 - 3y - 1 = (y+1)(4y^2 - 2y - 1)}}
S5. [theorem] A product is zero only if one factor is zero; y = cos 36 is not -1 because 36 degrees is not 180 degrees.
S6. [symbolic] Solve the quadratic factor -> {{4y^2 - 2y - 1 = 0 => y = (1 + sqrt(5))/4 or y = (1 - sqrt(5))/4}}
S7. [derive] Since 36 degrees is acute, cos 36 is positive, so y = (1 + sqrt(5))/4.
S8. [symbolic] Apply cos 72 = cos(2*36) = 2y^2 - 1 -> {{2((1+sqrt(5))/4)^2 - 1 => (sqrt(5)-1)/4}}

[Check]
V1. Substitute y = (1 + sqrt(5))/4 into 2y^2 - 1 and simplify to get (sqrt(5)-1)/4.
V2. The value (sqrt(5)-1)/4 is approximately 0.3090, which is between cos 60 = 1/2 and cos 90 = 0, as expected for cos 72.

[Answer]
\boxed{\frac{\sqrt5-1}{4}}

This is a vector projection problem. The goal is to find the projection of (4,1) onto a vector w, given the projection of (0,3) onto w. The key idea is that the given projection vector is parallel to w, so it can be used as the direction vector for the new projection.

[Plan]
P1. Recall the formula for projection onto a vector.
P2. Use the given projection to identify the direction of w.
P3. Compute the projection of the new vector onto that same direction.
P4. Verify that the result matches the projection formula.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let p = (-9/10, 3/10) and u = (4, 1). For nonzero w, the projection formula is proj_w(x) = ((x dot w)/(w dot w)) w.
S2. [derive] Since proj_w((0,3)) = p, p is a nonzero scalar multiple of w, so projecting onto w is the same as projecting onto p.
S3. [calc] Compute u dot p -> <<4*(-9/10)+1*(3/10)=-33/10>>.
S4. [calc] Compute p dot p -> <<(-9/10)^2+(3/10)^2=9/10>>.
S5. [calc] Compute the projection scalar -> <<(-33/10)/(9/10)=-11/3>>.
S6. [calc] Multiply the scalar by p -> <<(-11/3)*(-9/10,3/10)=(33/10,-11/10)>>.

[Check]
V1. The given projection p is parallel to w, so using p as the direction is valid.
V2. The scalar -11/3 times p gives (33/10, -11/10), matching the projection formula.

[Answer]
\boxed{\begin{pmatrix} 33/10 \\ -11/10 \end{pmatrix}}

[Overview]
This is a trigonometric sequence problem. The goal is to find the index n of the 100th negative cumulative sum a_n. The key idea is to rewrite a_n with the finite sine-sum formula and characterize when it is negative by a congruence condition modulo 2*pi.

[Plan]
P1. Write a_n using the finite sine-sum formula.
P2. Convert the sign condition a_n < 0 into an inequality for cos(n+1/2).
P3. Translate that inequality into interval conditions modulo 2*pi.
P4. Identify all integer indices n that make a_n negative.
P5. Count to the 100th such index and compute it.

[Solution]
S1. [setup] Let a_n = sum_{k=1}^n sin(k) and note that n is the index being counted.
S2. [theorem] The finite sine-sum identity gives sum_{k=1}^n sin(k) = sin(n/2) sin((n+1)/2) / sin(1/2).
S3. [symbolic] Use the product-to-sum identity -> {{sum_{k=1}^n sin(k) => (cos(1/2) - cos(n+1/2))/(2 sin(1/2))}}
S4. [derive] Since 2 sin(1/2) > 0, the inequality a_n < 0 is equivalent to cos(n+1/2) > cos(1/2).
S5. [derive] On the unit circle, cos(x) > cos(1/2) exactly when x is within distance 1/2 of a multiple of 2*pi, so n+1/2 must lie in (2*pi*m - 1/2, 2*pi*m + 1/2) for some integer m.
S6. [symbolic] Subtract 1/2 from all parts -> {{2*pi*m - 1/2 < n+1/2 < 2*pi*m + 1/2 => 2*pi*m - 1 < n < 2*pi*m}}
S7. [derive] For every positive integer m, the number 2*pi*m is not an integer, so the open interval (2*pi*m - 1, 2*pi*m) contains exactly one integer, namely floor(2*pi*m).
S8. [derive] Therefore the negative terms occur exactly at indices n = floor(2*pi*m) for m = 1, 2, 3, ... in increasing order, so the 100th negative term has index floor(2*pi*100).
S9. [calc] Compute the required index -> <<floor(2*pi*100)=628>>

[Check]
V1. For m = 1, the formula gives n = floor(2*pi) = 6; checking the sign condition at n = 6 gives cos(6.5) > cos(0.5), so a_6 < 0 as expected.
V2. The negative indices are one per value of m, and floor(2*pi*100) = 628. This index satisfies 2*pi*100 - 1 < 628 < 2*pi*100 because 200*pi is approximately 628.3185.

[Answer]
\boxed{628}
